kills.q: The 2004 Pacers-Pistons brawl known as the 'Malice at the Palace' took place at which arena?
kills.reason: The question text reveals its own answer. The event nickname quoted in the prompt ('Malice at the PALACE') hands the player the only option containing the word 'Palace' — The Palace of Auburn Hills — and the three distractors (Joe Louis Arena, Cobo Arena, Little Caesars Arena) are eliminable on the word alone with zero basketball knowledge. The marked answer is factually correct (the brawl was on Nov 19, 2004 at The Palace of Auburn Hills), so this is a giveaway problem, not a factual one, and it is unfixable without dropping the nickname that makes the question interesting.

kills.q: Who set the WNBA single-season rebounding record with 451 in 2024?
kills.reason: Ambiguous AND numerically wrong. Two of the four listed options legitimately 'set the WNBA single-season rebounding record in 2024': Angel Reese broke Sylvia Fowles' record on Sept 1, 2024 (finishing 446 in 34 games, plus she still holds the rpg record at 13.1), and A'ja Wilson then surpassed her on Sept 18, 2024. Headlines in 2024 credited BOTH, so a knowledgeable player can defensibly answer 'Angel Reese'. Worse, the disambiguating number is wrong: 451 was Wilson's total the night she passed Reese, not her season total — Wikipedia's career stat table lists her 2024 final at 452 rebounds (38 GP, 11.9 RPG). So the question as written describes a total that no player actually finished with. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A%27ja_Wilson , https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angel_Reese , https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Women%27s_National_Basketball_Association_annual_rebounding_leaders

fixes.q: How many career regular-season wins did Gregg Popovich retire with, the NBA record for a head coach?
fixes.problem: The marked answer 1,422 is wrong. Popovich retired in May 2025 with a career regular-season record of 1,390-824. Cross-check: he broke Don Nelson's record (1,335) with win #1,336 on March 11, 2022, then coached the remainder of 2021-22, all of 2022-23 (22 wins) and 2023-24 (22 wins), plus only ~5 games of 2024-25 before his stroke - which lands at ~1,390, not 1,422. The distractor 1,335 is actually Don Nelson's total. Replace the correct option with 1,390 and the other three distractors can stay.

facts.fact: The Philadelphia Warriors won the first championship of the Basketball Association of America (the league that became the NBA) in 1947, defeating the Chicago Stags in the Finals.

facts.subject: Rochester Royals
facts.fact: The Rochester Royals won the 1951 NBA championship, beating the New York Knicks in seven games and clinching on April 21, 1951. That franchise is today's Sacramento Kings.

facts.subject: Sacramento Kings
facts.fact: The Sacramento Kings franchise owns the NBA's longest championship drought: its only title came in 1951 as the Rochester Royals, over 75 years ago.

facts.subject: Syracuse Nationals
facts.fact: The Syracuse Nationals won the 1955 NBA title, the first season played with the 24-second shot clock, beating the Fort Wayne Pistons 92-91 in Game 7. It was the franchise's only title; it later became the Philadelphia 76ers.

facts.subject: Minneapolis Lakers
facts.fact: George Mikan's Minneapolis Lakers won five NBA championships in six seasons (1949, 1950, 1952, 1953, 1954), all coached by John Kundla.

facts.subject: Bob Pettit
facts.fact: Bob Pettit of the St. Louis Hawks won the first NBA Most Valuable Player award, for the 1955-56 season.

facts.subject: St. Louis Hawks
facts.fact: The St. Louis Hawks beat the Boston Celtics 4-2 in the 1958 NBA Finals for the franchise's only NBA championship. Bob Pettit scored 50 points in the clinching Game 6, and Alex Hannum coached the Hawks.

facts.subject: Bill Russell
facts.fact: The 1958 Finals was the only NBA Finals series Bill Russell ever lost; he finished 11-1 in the Finals and won 11 championships in 13 seasons.

facts.subject: Boston Celtics
facts.fact: The Boston Celtics won eight consecutive NBA championships from 1959 through 1966, the longest title streak in North American major professional sports.

facts.subject: Red Auerbach
facts.fact: Red Auerbach won nine NBA championships as head coach of the Boston Celtics (1957 and 1959-1966), a record that stood until Phil Jackson passed him in 2009.

facts.subject: Elgin Baylor
facts.fact: Elgin Baylor scored 61 points with 22 rebounds in Game 5 of the 1962 NBA Finals at Boston Garden — still the single-game scoring record in NBA Finals history.

facts.subject: Bill Russell
facts.fact: On April 17, 1966, Bill Russell was named head coach of the Boston Celtics, becoming the first Black head coach in the history of a major American professional sports league.

facts.subject: Bill Russell
facts.fact: Bill Russell won NBA championships in 1968 and 1969 as the Celtics' player-coach, making him the first Black head coach to win a title in a major North American pro league.

facts.subject: Jerry West
facts.fact: Jerry West won the first NBA Finals MVP award in 1969 even though his Lakers lost the series to Boston — he remains the only Finals MVP from the losing team.

facts.subject: Boston Celtics
facts.fact: The 1969 Celtics won the title as the East's fourth-place team at 48-34, beating the Lakers in seven games for Bill Russell's 11th and final championship.

facts.subject: Jack Kent Cooke
facts.fact: Lakers owner Jack Kent Cooke had thousands of celebration balloons hung in the Forum rafters before Game 7 of the 1969 Finals; Boston won 108-106 and the balloons were never released.

facts.subject: Willis Reed
facts.fact: Injured Knicks captain Willis Reed limped onto the Madison Square Garden floor before Game 7 of the 1970 Finals and hit New York's first two baskets; he was named Finals MVP as the Knicks won their first championship.

facts.subject: Walt Frazier
facts.fact: Walt Frazier posted 36 points and 19 assists in Game 7 of the 1970 NBA Finals as the Knicks beat the Lakers 113-99.

facts.subject: Milwaukee Bucks
facts.fact: The Milwaukee Bucks swept the Baltimore Bullets in the 1971 Finals in only their third season of existence — the fastest an expansion team has ever won a title. Lew Alcindor (Kareem Abdul-Jabbar) was Finals MVP, with Oscar Robertson alongside him.

facts.subject: Los Angeles Lakers
facts.fact: The 1971-72 Lakers won 33 consecutive games — still the longest winning streak in NBA history — and went on to win the franchise's first title in Los Angeles under coach Bill Sharman.
facts.volatileNote: Streak record could theoretically be broken.

facts.subject: Golden State Warriors
facts.fact: The 48-34 Golden State Warriors swept the 60-22 Washington Bullets in the 1975 NBA Finals; Rick Barry was Finals MVP, and it was the first championship series in major U.S. pro sports with two Black head coaches (Al Attles and K.C. Jones).

facts.subject: Portland Trail Blazers
facts.fact: The Portland Trail Blazers won their only NBA championship in 1977, losing the first two games to Philadelphia and then winning four straight; Bill Walton was Finals MVP.

facts.subject: Wes Unseld
facts.fact: Wes Unseld was named 1978 NBA Finals MVP while averaging only 9.0 points per game, as the Washington Bullets beat the Seattle SuperSonics in seven games.

facts.subject: Dick Motta
facts.fact: Bullets coach Dick Motta popularized the phrase 'the opera isn't over till the fat lady sings' during Washington's 1978 championship run.

facts.subject: Dennis Johnson
facts.fact: Dennis Johnson was Finals MVP when the Seattle SuperSonics beat Washington 4-1 in 1979 for the franchise's only NBA championship; Lenny Wilkens coached Seattle.

facts.subject: Magic Johnson

facts.subject: Cedric Maxwell

facts.subject: Philadelphia 76ers

facts.subject: Celtics-Lakers rivalry

facts.subject: Magic Johnson

facts.subject: James Worthy

facts.subject: Isiah Thomas

facts.subject: Detroit Pistons

facts.subject: Detroit Pistons

facts.subject: Hakeem Olajuwon

facts.subject: Boston Celtics

facts.subject: Los Angeles Lakers

facts.subject: Giannis Antetokounmpo

facts.subject: Boston Celtics

facts.subject: Jalen Brunson

facts.subject: John Salley

facts.subject: Klay Thompson
facts.fact: Klay Thompson scored an NBA-record 37 points in the third quarter against Sacramento on January 23, 2015, going 13-of-13 from the field including 9-of-9 from three; he finished with 52 in a 126-101 win.

facts.subject: Stephen Curry
facts.fact: Stephen Curry made 402 three-pointers in 2015-16, the single-season record; before that season no player had ever made 300 in a year, and the previous record was also Curry's.

facts.subject: Stephen Curry
facts.fact: Stephen Curry made at least one three-pointer in 268 consecutive regular-season games from December 1, 2018 to December 17, 2023, when he went 0-for-8 from deep against Portland. He also owns the second-longest such streak at 157 games.

facts.subject: Stephen Curry
facts.fact: Stephen Curry became the NBA's career three-point leader on December 14, 2021, passing Ray Allen's total of 2,973 made threes, and later became the first player to reach 4,000 career threes.
facts.volatileNote: Curry's career three-point total keeps rising while he is active.

facts.subject: John Stockton
facts.fact: John Stockton is the NBA's career assists leader with 15,806, more than 3,000 ahead of second place.

facts.subject: John Stockton
facts.fact: John Stockton is the NBA's career steals leader with 3,265, ahead of Chris Paul, Jason Kidd and Michael Jordan.

facts.subject: Hakeem Olajuwon
facts.fact: Hakeem Olajuwon is the NBA's career blocks leader with 3,830, ahead of Dikembe Mutombo (3,289) and Kareem Abdul-Jabbar (3,189).

facts.subject: Kareem Abdul-Jabbar
facts.fact: Kareem Abdul-Jabbar retired with 38,387 career points and held the NBA career scoring record for 38 years and 10 months, from 1984 to 2023.

facts.subject: LeBron James
facts.fact: LeBron James passed Kareem Abdul-Jabbar as the NBA's career regular-season scoring leader in February 2023 and has held the record since.
facts.volatileNote: LeBron's career point total rises while he is active.

facts.subject: NBA statistics
facts.fact: Blocked shots and steals were not tracked as official NBA statistics until the 1973-74 season, which is why no pre-1974 player appears on those career leaderboards.

facts.subject: Oscar Robertson
facts.fact: Oscar Robertson averaged 30.8 points, 12.5 rebounds and 11.4 assists over 79 games in 1961-62 — a triple-double for an entire season, in only his second NBA year.

facts.subject: Russell Westbrook
facts.fact: Russell Westbrook recorded 42 triple-doubles in 2016-17, breaking Oscar Robertson's 55-year-old single-season record of 41, and averaged 31.8 points, 10.7 rebounds and 10.4 assists on the way to MVP.

facts.subject: Russell Westbrook
facts.fact: Russell Westbrook is the NBA's career triple-double leader; he passed Oscar Robertson's long-standing mark of 181 on May 10, 2021 with his 182nd.
facts.volatileNote: Westbrook's total grows while active and Nikola Jokic is chasing it.

facts.subject: quadruple-doubles
facts.fact: Only four official quadruple-doubles have been recorded in NBA history: Nate Thurmond (1974), Alvin Robertson (1986), Hakeem Olajuwon (1990) and David Robinson (1994).
facts.volatileNote: A fifth quadruple-double would change the count.

facts.subject: Nate Thurmond
facts.fact: Nate Thurmond recorded the NBA's first official quadruple-double — 22 points, 14 rebounds, 13 assists and 12 blocks — in his Chicago Bulls debut on October 18, 1974, a 120-115 overtime win over Atlanta.

facts.subject: Alvin Robertson
facts.fact: Alvin Robertson's 1986 quadruple-double (20 points, 11 rebounds, 10 assists, 10 steals) is the only one in NBA history built on steals rather than blocks, and he is the only guard ever to record one.

facts.subject: Hakeem Olajuwon
facts.fact: Hakeem Olajuwon's 1990 quadruple-double was 18 points, 16 rebounds, 11 blocks and 10 assists in a 120-94 Rockets win.

facts.subject: David Robinson
facts.fact: David Robinson's 1994 quadruple-double was 34 points, 10 rebounds, 10 assists and 10 blocks — the only quadruple-double in NBA history with 30 or more points.

facts.subject: Alvin Robertson
facts.fact: Alvin Robertson set NBA single-season records with 301 steals and 3.67 steals per game for San Antonio in 1985-86, the year he won Defensive Player of the Year.

facts.subject: Mark Eaton
facts.fact: Mark Eaton blocked 456 shots (5.56 per game) for Utah in 1984-85, both single-season NBA records; his career average of 3.50 blocks per game is also an NBA record.

facts.subject: Manute Bol
facts.fact: Manute Bol is the only player in NBA history to retire with more career blocks (2,086) than career points (1,599); as a 7-foot-7 rookie in 1985-86 he averaged 5.0 blocks and only 3.7 points per game.

facts.subject: Hakeem Olajuwon
facts.fact: Hakeem Olajuwon has the most 5x5 games (at least five points, rebounds, assists, steals and blocks) with six; Andrei Kirilenko is next with three, and only about 22 have been recorded since blocks and steals became official in 1973-74.
facts.volatileNote: Active players such as Victor Wembanyama can add 5x5 games and change the leaderboard.

facts.subject: Moses Malone
facts.fact: Moses Malone is the NBA career leader in offensive rebounds with 6,731 since the stat became official in 1973-74 — more than 2,500 clear of second place — and he set the single-season record with 587 in 1978-79.

facts.subject: Dennis Rodman
facts.fact: Dennis Rodman won seven consecutive NBA rebounding titles from 1991-92 through 1997-98, starting with 18.7 rebounds per game (1,530 total) in 1991-92, and did it while playing for three different teams.

facts.subject: Charles Barkley
facts.fact: Charles Barkley led the NBA in rebounding in 1986-87 at 14.6 rebounds per game, the shortest player ever to win an NBA rebounding title.

facts.subject: Nate Archibald
facts.fact: Nate Archibald is the only player in NBA history to lead the league in both scoring (34.0 points per game) and assists (11.4 per game, 910 total) in the same season, doing it for Kansas City-Omaha in 1972-73.

facts.subject: Robert Parish
facts.fact: Robert Parish played 1,611 regular-season games, a career games-played record that stood until LeBron James passed it in March 2026; James finished the 2025-26 season on 1,622.
facts.volatileNote: LeBron's games-played total keeps rising while he is active.

facts.subject: A.C. Green
facts.fact: A.C. Green played 1,192 consecutive regular-season games between November 19, 1986 and April 18, 2001, the NBA iron-man record.

facts.subject: Kareem Abdul-Jabbar
facts.fact: Kareem Abdul-Jabbar's 57,446 career regular-season minutes stood as the NBA record from 1989 until LeBron James passed it; Abdul-Jabbar played 1,560 games over 20 seasons.
facts.volatileNote: LeBron James now holds the minutes record and his total keeps rising.

facts.subject: Micheal Williams
facts.fact: Micheal Williams of the Minnesota Timberwolves made 97 consecutive free throws over 19 games between March 24 and November 9, 1993, an NBA record; he broke Calvin Murphy's mark of 78.

facts.subject: 1971-72 Los Angeles Lakers
facts.fact: The Los Angeles Lakers won 33 straight games from November 5, 1971 to January 9, 1972, the longest winning streak in NBA history; Kareem Abdul-Jabbar's Milwaukee Bucks ended it 120-104.

facts.subject: Dale Ellis
facts.fact: Dale Ellis played 69 minutes — an NBA single-game record — in a five-overtime game on November 9, 1989 that Milwaukee won 155-154 over Seattle; he scored 53 points, and teammate Xavier McDaniel played 68 minutes.

facts.subject: Pistons-Nuggets 1983
facts.fact: Detroit beat Denver 186-184 in triple overtime on December 13, 1983 for 370 combined points, the highest-scoring game in NBA history; Kiki Vandeweghe scored 51, Isiah Thomas 47, Alex English 47 and John Long 41.

facts.subject: Kevin Love
facts.fact: Kevin Love had 31 points and 31 rebounds for Minnesota in a 112-103 win over the Knicks on November 12, 2010 — the NBA's first 30-point, 30-rebound game since Moses Malone on February 11, 1982. Love grabbed 15 boards in the third quarter alone.

facts.subject: Tony Delk
facts.fact: Tony Delk scored 53 points on 20-of-27 shooting for Phoenix at Sacramento on January 2, 2001 — the only 30-point game of his 10-year, 9.1-points-per-game career; the Suns still lost 121-117 in overtime.

facts.subject: Willie Burton
facts.fact: Willie Burton scored 53 points for the Philadelphia 76ers against Miami on December 13, 1994 in a 105-90 win, needing only 19 field goal attempts: 12 made field goals including five threes, plus a franchise-record 24 free throws.

facts.subject: Brandon Jennings
facts.fact: Rookie Brandon Jennings scored 55 points in just his seventh NBA game, on November 14, 2009 against Golden State, after a scoreless first quarter and a 29-point third quarter.

facts.subject: Jamal Crawford
facts.fact: Jamal Crawford scored 51 points off the bench for Phoenix against Dallas on April 9, 2019 at age 39 — the most points ever scored by a reserve and the oldest 50-point game in NBA history, breaking Michael Jordan's age mark.
facts.volatileNote: 'Oldest' and 'most by a reserve' marks can be broken.

facts.subject: Michael Jordan
facts.fact: Michael Jordan won a record 10 NBA scoring titles; Wilt Chamberlain is second with seven, all consecutive from 1960 through 1966.

facts.subject: Michael Jordan
facts.fact: Michael Jordan's career scoring average of 30.12 points per game is the highest in NBA history, narrowly ahead of Wilt Chamberlain's 30.07.
facts.volatileNote: An active player could in principle finish a career above 30.12.

facts.subject: Michael Jordan
facts.fact: Michael Jordan scored 63 points at Boston Garden on April 20, 1986 in a 135-131 double-overtime playoff loss — still the NBA postseason single-game scoring record. He shot 22-of-41 from the field and 19-of-21 from the line, breaking Elgin Baylor's 61.

facts.subject: Elgin Baylor
facts.fact: Elgin Baylor scored 61 points with 22 rebounds in Game 5 of the 1962 NBA Finals at Boston on April 14, 1962, a 126-121 Lakers win — still the NBA Finals single-game scoring record.

facts.subject: Bill Russell
facts.fact: Bill Russell holds the NBA Finals single-game rebounding record with 40, which he reached in Game 2 of the 1960 Finals and again in a 30-point, 40-rebound Game 7 of the 1962 Finals.

facts.subject: Bill Russell
facts.fact: Bill Russell's 51 rebounds against the Syracuse Nationals on February 5, 1960 is the second-highest single-game rebounding total in NBA history, behind only Wilt Chamberlain's 55.

facts.subject: Shai Gilgeous-Alexander
facts.fact: Shai Gilgeous-Alexander scored at least 20 points in 127 consecutive games, breaking Wilt Chamberlain's record of 126 that had stood since 1963. He set the mark on March 12, 2026 with 35 points and nine assists in a 104-102 Thunder win over Boston.
facts.volatileNote: The streak length keeps growing while it is alive and can be extended or broken.

facts.subject: Luka Doncic
facts.fact: Luka Doncic led the NBA in scoring in the 2025-26 season at 33.5 points per game, ahead of Shai Gilgeous-Alexander's 31.1.

facts.subject: Wilt Chamberlain
facts.fact: On March 2, 1962, Wilt Chamberlain scored 100 points for the Philadelphia Warriors in a 169-147 win over the New York Knicks at the Hershey Sports Arena in Hershey, Pennsylvania. He shot 36-of-63 from the field and made 28 of 32 free throws.

facts.subject: Bam Adebayo
facts.fact: On March 10, 2026, Bam Adebayo scored 83 points for the Miami Heat in a 150-129 win over the Washington Wizards at Kaseya Center. He shot 20-of-43 from the field, 7-of-22 from three and set the NBA single-game record with 36 free throws made on 43 attempts. It is the second-highest single-game total in NBA history behind Chamberlain's 100.
facts.volatileNote: Its rank as the second-highest single-game total can change if another player scores 84+.

facts.subject: Kobe Bryant
facts.fact: On January 22, 2006, Kobe Bryant scored 81 points in a 122-104 Lakers win over the Toronto Raptors, going 28-of-46 from the field and 7-of-13 from three. He scored 55 of those points in the second half after the Lakers trailed by 18 in the third quarter.

facts.subject: Michael Jordan
facts.fact: On April 20, 1986, Michael Jordan scored 63 points at Boston Garden in Game 2 of a first-round playoff series — still the NBA playoff single-game record — but the Celtics won 135-131 in double overtime. Larry Bird said afterward, 'I think it's just God disguised as Michael Jordan.'

facts.subject: Klay Thompson
facts.fact: On January 23, 2015, Klay Thompson scored an NBA-record 37 points in the third quarter against the Sacramento Kings, going 13-of-13 from the field and 9-of-9 from three. He finished with 52 points in a 126-101 Warriors win.

facts.subject: Devin Booker
facts.fact: On March 24, 2017, 20-year-old Devin Booker scored 70 points at TD Garden in Boston, going 21-of-40 from the field and 24-of-26 from the line, but the Suns lost to the Celtics 130-120.

facts.subject: Michael Jordan
facts.fact: On June 11, 1997, a visibly ill Michael Jordan scored 38 points in 44 minutes in Game 5 of the NBA Finals in Utah, leading the Bulls to a 90-88 win in what became known as the 'Flu Game.'

facts.subject: Michael Jordan
facts.fact: On May 7, 1989, Michael Jordan hit 'The Shot' at the buzzer over Craig Ehlo in Game 5 of the first round, giving the Bulls a 101-100 win that eliminated the Cleveland Cavaliers. It was his 43rd and 44th points of the game.

facts.subject: Ray Allen
facts.fact: In Game 6 of the 2013 NBA Finals, with Miami trailing San Antonio 95-92 and 5.2 seconds left, Chris Bosh rebounded a LeBron James miss and passed to Ray Allen, whose corner three tied the game. The Heat won 103-100 in overtime and took the title in Game 7.

facts.subject: Kawhi Leonard
facts.fact: On May 12, 2019, Kawhi Leonard hit a corner jumper over Joel Embiid that bounced on the rim four times before dropping, giving Toronto a 92-90 Game 7 win over Philadelphia — the first game-winning buzzer-beater in a Game 7 in NBA history. Leonard scored 41 points.

facts.subject: Damian Lillard
facts.fact: On April 23, 2019, Damian Lillard ended Portland's first-round series with a 37-foot buzzer-beater over Paul George in a 118-115 Game 5 win over Oklahoma City. Lillard scored 50 points and waved goodbye to the Thunder bench.

facts.subject: Derek Fisher
facts.fact: On May 13, 2004, after Tim Duncan's fadeaway put San Antonio ahead 73-72 with 0.4 seconds left, Derek Fisher caught and shot in one motion to win Game 5 of the Western Conference semifinals 74-73 for the Lakers.

facts.subject: Steve Kerr
facts.fact: In Game 6 of the 1997 NBA Finals, tied 86-86, Michael Jordan drew John Stockton's help defense and passed to Steve Kerr, whose 17-foot jumper with five seconds left put Chicago ahead. The Bulls beat Utah 90-86 for their fifth title.

facts.subject: Robert Horry
facts.fact: In Game 5 of the 2005 NBA Finals, Robert Horry scored 21 points — 18 of them in the fourth quarter and overtime — and hit a three with 5.8 seconds left in OT for a 96-95 Spurs win over Detroit. He went 5-of-6 from three.

facts.subject: John Havlicek
facts.fact: On April 15, 1965, with Boston leading Philadelphia 110-109 and five seconds left in Game 7 of the Eastern Division Finals, John Havlicek tipped away Hal Greer's inbounds pass. Radio announcer Johnny Most's call — 'Havlicek stole the ball!' — is regarded by the NBA as the most famous radio call in basketball history.

facts.subject: LeBron James
facts.fact: In Game 7 of the 2016 NBA Finals at Oracle Arena, with the score tied 89-89 inside two minutes, LeBron James chased down and pinned Andre Iguodala's layup against the backboard. Kyrie Irving then hit the go-ahead three as Cleveland won the title.

facts.subject: Reggie Miller
facts.fact: On May 7, 1995, at Madison Square Garden, Reggie Miller scored 8 points in about 9 seconds — a three, a steal and another three, then two free throws — to erase a six-point deficit and beat the Knicks 107-105 in Game 1 of the Eastern Conference semifinals.

facts.subject: Tracy McGrady
facts.fact: On December 9, 2004, Tracy McGrady scored 13 points in the final 35 seconds — four straight three-pointers, one a four-point play over Tim Duncan — to give Houston an 81-80 win over San Antonio.

facts.subject: Magic Johnson
facts.fact: On May 16, 1980, with Kareem Abdul-Jabbar sidelined by an ankle injury, rookie Magic Johnson started at center in Game 6 of the NBA Finals and posted 42 points, 15 rebounds and 7 assists in a 123-107 title-clinching win over Philadelphia. He remains the only rookie to win Finals MVP.

facts.subject: Allen Iverson
facts.fact: On March 12, 1997, rookie Allen Iverson double-crossed Michael Jordan and hit a jumper over him, scoring 37 points in a 108-104 Sixers loss to the Bulls. The move became one of the most replayed highlights of the era.

facts.subject: 1984 NBA Draft
facts.fact: In the 1984 NBA Draft, Houston took Hakeem Olajuwon first, Portland took Kentucky center Sam Bowie second, and Chicago took Michael Jordan third. Charles Barkley went fifth to Philadelphia. Bowie's Portland career was wrecked by leg injuries, making the pick one of the most second-guessed in league history.

facts.subject: Kobe Bryant
facts.fact: The Charlotte Hornets selected 17-year-old Kobe Bryant 13th overall in the 1996 NBA Draft and traded him to the Los Angeles Lakers for center Vlade Divac. Divac threatened to retire rather than be dealt, and the trade was not officially completed until July 11, 1996.

facts.subject: 2003 NBA Draft
facts.fact: The 2003 NBA Draft opened LeBron James (Cleveland), Darko Milicic (Detroit), Carmelo Anthony (Denver), Chris Bosh (Toronto) and Dwyane Wade (Miami). Four of the top five became Hall of Famers; Milicic is the outlier.

facts.subject: Greg Oden
facts.fact: Portland took Greg Oden first overall in the 2007 draft and Seattle took Kevin Durant second. Oden had microfracture surgery on his right knee on September 13, 2007 and missed his entire rookie season; he played only 105 NBA games in his career.

facts.subject: Kwame Brown
facts.fact: The Washington Wizards, with Michael Jordan running basketball operations, took Kwame Brown first overall in the 2001 draft — the first player ever selected No. 1 straight out of high school. Brown averaged 4.5 points and 3.5 rebounds as a rookie.

facts.subject: Anthony Bennett
facts.fact: Cleveland took UNLV forward Anthony Bennett first overall in the 2013 draft. He played 52 games as a rookie and averaged 4.2 points and 3.0 rebounds, and was out of the NBA within four seasons.

facts.subject: LaRue Martin
facts.fact: Portland used the No. 1 pick in the 1972 NBA Draft on Loyola-Chicago center LaRue Martin, ahead of Bob McAdoo (2nd) and Julius Erving (12th). Martin lasted four seasons and averaged 5.3 points and 4.6 rebounds.

facts.subject: Frederic Weis
facts.fact: The New York Knicks used the 15th pick of the 1999 draft on 7-foot-2 French center Frederic Weis, who never played a single NBA game. Queens native Ron Artest was taken with the very next pick, 16th, by Chicago. Weis was later the victim of Vince Carter's 'Dunk of Death' at the 2000 Olympics.

facts.subject: Nikola Jokic
facts.fact: Denver selected Nikola Jokic 41st overall in the 2014 NBA Draft. His name appeared on the broadcast ticker while a Taco Bell Quesarito commercial was airing, and Jokic was asleep in Serbia when his family woke him with the news.

facts.subject: Manu Ginobili
facts.fact: San Antonio selected Manu Ginobili with the 57th pick of the 1999 NBA Draft. He stayed in Europe for three more seasons and did not debut for the Spurs until age 25, then won four championships.

facts.subject: Isaiah Thomas
facts.fact: Sacramento took 5-foot-9 Isaiah Thomas with the 60th and final pick of the 2011 NBA Draft, earning him the 'Mr. Irrelevant' tag. He became a two-time All-Star with Boston.

facts.subject: Draymond Green
facts.fact: Golden State drafted Draymond Green 35th overall in 2012 out of Michigan State, where he was the school's all-time leading rebounder and 2012 Big Ten Player of the Year.

facts.subject: Giannis Antetokounmpo
facts.fact: Milwaukee selected Giannis Antetokounmpo 15th overall in the 2013 NBA Draft out of the Greek second division. His combination of size, speed and handle earned him the nickname 'Greek Freak.'

facts.subject: Dennis Rodman
facts.fact: Detroit drafted Dennis Rodman 27th overall in the second round of the 1986 NBA Draft out of Southeastern Oklahoma State. He became a two-time champion with the Bad Boys Pistons and later a three-time champion with the Bulls.

facts.subject: 1985 NBA Draft Lottery
facts.fact: The 1985 draft lottery was the first ever held. The New York Knicks won it and selected Georgetown center Patrick Ewing first overall, spawning the enduring 'frozen envelope' conspiracy theory that the league marked New York's envelope so commissioner David Stern could identify it.

facts.subject: Victor Wembanyama
facts.fact: Victor Wembanyama won 2023-24 Rookie of the Year unanimously with all 99 first-place votes, averaging 21.4 points, 10.6 rebounds, 3.9 assists and 3.6 blocks in 71 games for San Antonio. Chet Holmgren finished runner-up.

facts.subject: Wilt Chamberlain
facts.fact: In 1959-60 Wilt Chamberlain averaged 37.6 points and 27.0 rebounds for the Philadelphia Warriors, leading the league in both, and won Rookie of the Year and MVP in the same season.

facts.subject: Michael Jordan
facts.fact: Michael Jordan averaged 28.2 points, 6.5 rebounds, 5.9 assists and 2.4 steals as a rookie in 1984-85 and won Rookie of the Year, finishing third in the league in scoring behind Bernard King and Larry Bird.

facts.subject: LeBron James
facts.fact: LeBron James made his NBA debut on October 29, 2003 at Sacramento, scoring 25 points with 6 rebounds, 9 assists and 4 steals on 12-of-20 shooting at age 18. The Cavaliers lost 106-92.

facts.subject: Scottie Pippen
facts.fact: Seattle drafted Scottie Pippen out of Central Arkansas fifth overall in 1987 and traded him to Chicago for the rights to Olden Polynice (the No. 8 pick) plus draft picks. Pippen became a six-time champion.

facts.subject: Dirk Nowitzki
facts.fact: Milwaukee selected Dirk Nowitzki ninth overall in the 1998 draft and immediately traded him to Dallas for the rights to Robert 'Tractor' Traylor, the No. 6 pick. Traylor lasted seven NBA seasons; Nowitzki became a Finals MVP and Hall of Famer.

facts.subject: Kareem Abdul-Jabbar
facts.fact: On June 16, 1975, Milwaukee traded Kareem Abdul-Jabbar and Walt Wesley to the Los Angeles Lakers for Elmore Smith, Brian Winters, Junior Bridgeman and Dave Meyers. Abdul-Jabbar won five titles in Los Angeles.

facts.subject: Moses Malone
facts.fact: Philadelphia signed Moses Malone to an offer sheet in September 1982; unable to match, Houston agreed to a sign-and-trade on September 15, 1982, receiving Caldwell Jones and a 1983 first-round pick. Malone won MVP and the 1983 title in Philadelphia after predicting the playoffs would go 'Fo', fo', fo'.'

facts.subject: Charles Barkley
facts.fact: On June 19, 1992, Philadelphia traded Charles Barkley to the Phoenix Suns for Jeff Hornacek, Tim Perry and Andrew Lang. Barkley won MVP in his first season in Phoenix and reached the 1993 Finals.

facts.subject: Shaquille O'Neal
facts.fact: On July 14, 2004, weeks after the Lakers lost the Finals to Detroit, Los Angeles traded Shaquille O'Neal to the Miami Heat for Lamar Odom, Caron Butler, Brian Grant and a future first-round pick. O'Neal won his fourth title in Miami in 2006.

facts.subject: Kevin Garnett
facts.fact: On July 31, 2007, Boston sent Al Jefferson, Ryan Gomes, Gerald Green, Sebastian Telfair, Theo Ratliff, two first-round picks and cash to Minnesota for Kevin Garnett — the largest package ever assembled for a single player. Al Jefferson was the piece Minnesota insisted on.

facts.subject: Chris Paul
facts.fact: On December 8, 2011, commissioner David Stern vetoed an agreed three-team trade that would have sent Chris Paul from the league-owned New Orleans Hornets to the Lakers, citing 'basketball reasons.' Paul was traded to the Clippers a week later.

facts.subject: 2018 NBA Draft
facts.fact: On draft night 2018 Atlanta selected Luka Doncic third and Dallas selected Trae Young fifth, then swapped: Dallas got Doncic and sent Atlanta Young plus a protected 2019 first-round pick.

facts.subject: Luka Doncic
facts.fact: On the night of February 1-2, 2025, Dallas traded Luka Doncic, Maxi Kleber and Markieff Morris to the Lakers for Anthony Davis, Max Christie and a 2029 first-round pick, with Utah as a third team. It was the first time two reigning All-NBA players were traded for each other in midseason.

facts.subject: Kobe Bryant
facts.fact: Kobe Bryant adopted the 'Black Mamba' alter ego around 2003, taking the name from Quentin Tarantino's film Kill Bill, in which the black mamba snake is an assassin's code name.

facts.subject: Paul Pierce
facts.fact: Shaquille O'Neal gave Paul Pierce the nickname 'The Truth' after Pierce scored 42 against the Lakers on March 13, 2001, telling a Boston Herald reporter to quote him that Pierce was the truth.

facts.subject: Gary Payton
facts.fact: Gary Payton got the nickname 'The Glove' from his cousin Glen during the 1993 Western Conference Finals, after Payton smothered Phoenix's Kevin Johnson — 'you got Kevin Johnson like a baseball in a glove.'

facts.subject: Tim Duncan
facts.fact: Shaquille O'Neal gave Tim Duncan the nickname 'The Big Fundamental,' explaining that Duncan's fundamental skills were perfect and comparing him to Larry Bird.

facts.subject: Dennis Rodman
facts.fact: Dennis Rodman's nickname 'The Worm' is traced to his mother watching him wriggle while playing pinball as a boy, and to his knack for squirming after loose balls.

facts.subject: Bill Russell
facts.fact: On August 11, 2022, the NBA retired Bill Russell's No. 6 league-wide, the first number ever retired across the entire league. Players already wearing No. 6, such as LeBron James, were allowed to keep it.

facts.subject: Michael Jordan
facts.fact: Michael Jordan announced his return from his first retirement with a two-word statement — 'I'm back' — on March 18, 1995, and played the next night against the Indiana Pacers wearing No. 45 because the Bulls had retired his No. 23.

facts.subject: Kobe Bryant
facts.fact: Kobe Bryant wore No. 8 from 1996 through 2005-06 and switched to No. 24 starting in 2006-07. On December 18, 2017 the Lakers retired both numbers, making him the first player to have two numbers retired by the same team.

facts.subject: Boston Celtics parquet floor
facts.fact: The Celtics' famous parquet floor was created in 1946 because a post-World War II shortage of long lumber forced builders to use short scraps of red oak, assembled into 247 five-foot-square panels laid in alternating directions. It was first installed at Boston Arena and moved to Boston Garden in 1952.

facts.subject: NBA logo
facts.fact: The NBA's logo was designed by Alan Siegel in 1969 using a Sport magazine photograph of Lakers guard Jerry West dribbling with his left hand. The league has never officially confirmed that the silhouette is West.

facts.subject: Malice at the Palace
facts.fact: On November 19, 2004 at The Palace of Auburn Hills, with Indiana leading Detroit 97-82 and 45.9 seconds left, a foul on Ben Wallace triggered a player-and-fan brawl. Ron Artest was suspended for the remaining 73 games of the season (86 including playoffs), Stephen Jackson 30, Jermaine O'Neal 25 (reduced to 15 on appeal), Anthony Johnson 5 and Ben Wallace 6.

facts.subject: Seattle SuperSonics relocation
facts.fact: After Clay Bennett's Oklahoma group bought the Seattle SuperSonics in 2006 and failed to secure a new arena, a July 2, 2008 settlement let the team move for $45 million. Seattle retained the SuperSonics name, colors and history; the team became the Oklahoma City Thunder for 2008-09.

facts.subject: Michael Jordan
facts.fact: At the 1988 Slam Dunk Contest in Chicago on February 6, Michael Jordan won his second straight title by taking off from the free-throw line for a perfect 50, edging Dominique Wilkins in a finish Wilkins still disputes.

facts.subject: Spud Webb
facts.fact: On February 8, 1986 in Dallas, 5-foot-7 Atlanta Hawks guard Spud Webb won the Slam Dunk Contest, beating his own teammate and defending champion Dominique Wilkins.

facts.subject: Vince Carter
facts.fact: Vince Carter won the 2000 Slam Dunk Contest in Oakland, opening with a reverse 360 windmill for a perfect 50 and later hanging with his forearm through the rim. He beat out Steve Francis and his cousin and then-teammate Tracy McGrady.

facts.subject: 2016 Slam Dunk Contest
facts.fact: At the 2016 Slam Dunk Contest in Toronto, Zach LaVine beat Aaron Gordon after both posted perfect 50s through two tiebreaker rounds. Gordon's under-the-legs dunk over the spinning Orlando Magic mascot is widely called the best dunk in contest history; LaVine clinched it with a between-the-legs dunk from the free-throw line.

facts.subject: Magic Johnson
facts.fact: On February 9, 1992 at the Orlando Arena, Magic Johnson — retired months earlier after announcing he was HIV-positive but still voted in as a starter — scored 25 points with 9 assists and won All-Star Game MVP as the West won 153-113.

facts.subject: 2020 NBA All-Star Game
facts.fact: The 2020 All-Star Game at Chicago's United Center on February 16 debuted the Elam Ending: the target score was the leading team's three-quarter total (Team Giannis had 133) plus 24 in tribute to Kobe Bryant, making it 157. Team LeBron won 157-155 on an Anthony Davis free throw.

facts.subject: 1997 inaugural game
facts.fact: The first WNBA regular-season game was played June 21, 1997 at the Great Western Forum in Los Angeles, where the New York Liberty beat the Los Angeles Sparks 67-57 before 14,284 fans.

facts.subject: Penny Toler
facts.fact: Los Angeles Sparks guard Penny Toler scored the first basket in WNBA history, in the league's opening game on June 21, 1997.

facts.subject: 1997 WNBA season
facts.fact: The WNBA launched in 1997 with eight teams: the Charlotte Sting, Cleveland Rockers, Houston Comets, Los Angeles Sparks, New York Liberty, Phoenix Mercury, Sacramento Monarchs and Utah Starzz. Each team played a 28-game schedule.

facts.subject: 1997 Houston Comets
facts.fact: The Houston Comets won the first WNBA championship on August 30, 1997, beating the New York Liberty 65-51 in a single winner-take-all championship game.

facts.subject: Houston Comets
facts.fact: The Houston Comets won the WNBA's first four championships, in 1997, 1998, 1999 and 2000, under head coach Van Chancellor.

facts.subject: Cynthia Cooper
facts.fact: Cynthia Cooper was named WNBA Finals MVP in all four of Houston's championship seasons (1997, 1998, 1999, 2000).

facts.subject: Cynthia Cooper
facts.fact: Cynthia Cooper won the WNBA's first regular-season MVP award in 1997, receiving all 37 first-place votes.

facts.subject: Cynthia Cooper
facts.fact: Cynthia Cooper-Dyke was inducted into the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame in 2010, the first WNBA player to be enshrined there.

facts.subject: Sheryl Swoopes
facts.fact: Sheryl Swoopes missed the first 19 games of the WNBA's 1997 season because she gave birth to her son Jordan on June 25, 1997 — four days after the league's first game. She debuted on August 7, six weeks after delivery.

facts.subject: Kim Perrot
facts.fact: Houston Comets guard Kim Perrot died of cancer in 1999 at age 32; the Comets dedicated their 1999 title to her and retired her No. 10.

facts.subject: 1999 WNBA All-Star Game
facts.fact: The first WNBA All-Star Game was held July 14, 1999 at Madison Square Garden, with the West beating the East 79-61.

facts.subject: Tina Thompson
facts.fact: USC forward Tina Thompson was the No. 1 overall selection of the WNBA's first college draft in April 1997, taken by the Houston Comets.

facts.subject: Margo Dydek
facts.fact: Poland's Margo Dydek was the No. 1 overall pick of the 1998 WNBA draft, taken by the Utah Starzz. At 7-foot-2 she is the tallest player in WNBA history.

facts.subject: Margo Dydek
facts.fact: Margo Dydek retired in 2008 as the WNBA's career blocks leader with 877 and led the league in blocks nine times. Brittney Griner has since passed her total.
facts.volatileNote: Griner is active and still adding blocks; the career leader's total keeps rising.

facts.subject: Tracy Reid
facts.fact: Charlotte Sting forward Tracy Reid won the WNBA's first Rookie of the Year award, presented in 1998.

facts.subject: Chamique Holdsclaw
facts.fact: Tennessee's Chamique Holdsclaw was the No. 1 overall pick of the 1999 WNBA draft by the Washington Mystics, and won Rookie of the Year that season.

facts.subject: Chamique Holdsclaw
facts.fact: Chamique Holdsclaw set the WNBA single-game rebounding record with 24 boards for Washington at Charlotte on May 23, 2003.
facts.volatileNote: A single-game record that could be broken.

facts.subject: Orlando Miracle
facts.fact: The Orlando Miracle and Minnesota Lynx joined the WNBA as expansion teams in 1999. The Miracle relocated to Uncasville, Connecticut in 2003 and were renamed the Sun after the Mohegan tribe's Mohegan Sun casino.

facts.subject: Ann Wauters
facts.fact: Belgian center Ann Wauters was the No. 1 overall pick of the 2000 WNBA draft, selected by the Cleveland Rockers.

facts.subject: Jackie Stiles
facts.fact: Jackie Stiles won the 2001 WNBA Rookie of the Year award playing for the Portland Fire, a franchise that folded after the 2002 season.

facts.subject: Los Angeles Sparks
facts.fact: The Los Angeles Sparks won back-to-back WNBA titles in 2001 and 2002, with Lisa Leslie named Finals MVP both years.

facts.subject: Lisa Leslie
facts.fact: Lisa Leslie recorded the first dunk in a WNBA game on July 30, 2002, playing for the Los Angeles Sparks against the Miami Sol.

facts.subject: 2003 Detroit Shock
facts.fact: The Detroit Shock went 9-23 in 2002 and then 25-9 in 2003 and won the title under Bill Laimbeer — the first worst-to-first turnaround in WNBA history.

facts.subject: Ruth Riley
facts.fact: Ruth Riley was named 2003 WNBA Finals MVP, scoring a career-high 27 points in the decisive Game 3 as Detroit beat the two-time defending champion Los Angeles Sparks 83-78.

facts.subject: 2003 WNBA Finals
facts.fact: Game 3 of the 2003 WNBA Finals at The Palace of Auburn Hills drew 22,076 fans, a WNBA attendance record at the time.
facts.volatileNote: Attendance records have since been challenged by neutral-site and expansion games.

facts.subject: Ticha Penicheiro
facts.fact: Ticha Penicheiro recorded 10 steals for Sacramento against San Antonio on July 10, 2003 — the only 10-steal game in WNBA history.
facts.volatileNote: A single-game mark that could be matched or broken.

facts.subject: 2004 Seattle Storm
facts.fact: The Seattle Storm won their first WNBA championship in 2004, beating the Connecticut Sun 2-1, with Betty Lennox named Finals MVP.

facts.subject: 2005 Sacramento Monarchs
facts.fact: The Sacramento Monarchs won their only WNBA championship in 2005, beating Connecticut 3-1, with Yolanda Griffith named Finals MVP. The franchise folded in 2009.

facts.subject: Deanna Nolan
facts.fact: Deanna Nolan was named WNBA Finals MVP in 2006 as the Detroit Shock beat the Sacramento Monarchs 3-2.

facts.subject: 2007 Phoenix Mercury
facts.fact: The Phoenix Mercury won their first WNBA title in 2007, beating Detroit 3-2, with Cappie Pondexter named Finals MVP.

facts.subject: Katie Smith
facts.fact: Katie Smith was named WNBA Finals MVP in 2008 as the Detroit Shock swept the San Antonio Silver Stars 3-0 for Detroit's third title.

facts.subject: Candace Parker
facts.fact: Candace Parker won both Rookie of the Year and regular-season MVP in 2008, the only player in WNBA history to take both awards in the same season.

facts.subject: Lauren Jackson
facts.fact: Australian forward Lauren Jackson won three WNBA MVP awards with the Seattle Storm, in 2003, 2007 and 2010.

facts.subject: 2010 Seattle Storm
facts.fact: The Seattle Storm swept the Atlanta Dream 3-0 for the 2010 WNBA title, with Lauren Jackson named Finals MVP.

facts.subject: 2011 Tulsa Shock
facts.fact: The 2011 Tulsa Shock finished 3-31, the worst single-season record and lowest winning percentage (.088) in WNBA history.

facts.subject: Minnesota Lynx
facts.fact: The Minnesota Lynx won four WNBA championships — 2011, 2013, 2015 and 2017 — reaching six Finals in seven seasons from 2011 to 2017 under coach Cheryl Reeve, built around Seimone Augustus, Maya Moore, Rebekkah Brunson, Lindsay Whalen and later Sylvia Fowles.

facts.subject: 2012 Indiana Fever
facts.fact: The Indiana Fever won their only WNBA championship in 2012, beating the Minnesota Lynx 3-1, with Tamika Catchings named Finals MVP.
facts.volatileNote: 'Only title' changes if Indiana wins another championship.

facts.subject: Tamika Catchings
facts.fact: Tamika Catchings is the WNBA's all-time steals leader with 1,074, played all 15 of her seasons with the Indiana Fever, and won a record five Defensive Player of the Year awards.

facts.subject: Brittney Griner
facts.fact: Baylor's Brittney Griner was the No. 1 overall pick of the 2013 WNBA draft, taken by the Phoenix Mercury.

facts.subject: Brittney Griner
facts.fact: In her WNBA debut on May 27, 2013, Brittney Griner dunked twice, becoming the first player to dunk twice in a single WNBA game.

facts.subject: Brittney Griner
facts.fact: Brittney Griner set the WNBA single-game blocks record with 11 for Phoenix at Tulsa on June 29, 2014.
facts.volatileNote: Single-game record that could be broken.

facts.subject: 2014 Phoenix Mercury
facts.fact: The 2014 Phoenix Mercury went 29-5 in the regular season and swept Chicago in the Finals; their .853 winning percentage remains the best in WNBA history.
facts.volatileNote: Best winning percentage could be surpassed.

facts.subject: Sylvia Fowles
facts.fact: Sylvia Fowles was named WNBA Finals MVP for the Minnesota Lynx in both 2015 and 2017, and was regular-season MVP in 2017.

facts.subject: Nneka Ogwumike
facts.fact: Nneka Ogwumike won the 2016 WNBA MVP with the Los Angeles Sparks, the same season she hit the title-winning shot in Game 5 of the Finals against Minnesota; Candace Parker was Finals MVP.

facts.subject: Kelsey Plum
facts.fact: Washington's Kelsey Plum was the No. 1 overall pick of the 2017 WNBA draft, taken by the San Antonio Stars a year before the franchise relocated to Las Vegas.

facts.subject: Liz Cambage
facts.fact: Liz Cambage scored 53 points for the Dallas Wings against the New York Liberty on July 17, 2018, setting the WNBA single-game scoring record. A'ja Wilson (2023) and Marina Mabrey (2026) have since matched it.
facts.volatileNote: 53 is the current single-game ceiling; it can be broken or matched again.

facts.subject: Elena Delle Donne
facts.fact: Elena Delle Donne won WNBA MVP with two franchises — the Chicago Sky in 2015 and the Washington Mystics in 2019.

facts.subject: Elena Delle Donne
facts.fact: In 2019 Elena Delle Donne became the first WNBA player to shoot 50/40/90 in a season, finishing at 51.5% from the field, 43.0% on threes and 97.4% at the line.

facts.subject: Emma Meesseman
facts.fact: Belgian forward Emma Meesseman won 2019 Finals MVP off the bench as the Washington Mystics won their first title, the first bench player to take the award.

facts.subject: 2020 WNBA season
facts.fact: The 2020 WNBA season was played in a COVID-19 bubble — the 'Wubble' — at IMG Academy in Bradenton, Florida, and was dedicated to Breonna Taylor and the Say Her Name campaign.

facts.subject: Crystal Dangerfield
facts.fact: Minnesota's Crystal Dangerfield, the 16th overall pick, became the first second-round draft pick to win WNBA Rookie of the Year, in 2020.

facts.subject: Sabrina Ionescu
facts.fact: Oregon's Sabrina Ionescu was the No. 1 overall pick of the 2020 WNBA draft, taken by the New York Liberty.

facts.subject: Jonquel Jones
facts.fact: Bahamian forward Jonquel Jones won the 2021 WNBA MVP award with the Connecticut Sun.

facts.subject: 2021 Chicago Sky
facts.fact: The Chicago Sky won their first WNBA championship in 2021, beating the Phoenix Mercury 3-1, with Kahleah Copper named Finals MVP.

facts.subject: Charli Collier
facts.fact: Texas center Charli Collier was the No. 1 overall pick of the 2021 WNBA draft, taken by the Dallas Wings.

facts.subject: 2022 Las Vegas Aces
facts.fact: The Las Vegas Aces won the 2022 WNBA title — the franchise's first and Las Vegas's first major pro sports championship — sweeping Connecticut 3-0 with Chelsea Gray named Finals MVP.

facts.subject: Las Vegas Aces
facts.fact: The Las Vegas Aces franchise began in 1997 as the Utah Starzz, moved to San Antonio in 2003 (Silver Stars, later Stars), and relocated to Las Vegas in 2018.

facts.subject: Dallas Wings
facts.fact: The Dallas Wings franchise played as the Detroit Shock from 1998 to 2009, the Tulsa Shock from 2010 to 2015, and became the Dallas Wings in 2016.

facts.subject: Diana Taurasi
facts.fact: Diana Taurasi became the first WNBA player to reach 10,000 career points on August 3, 2023, scoring a season-high 42 against Atlanta. She retired as the all-time leading scorer with 10,646 points.

facts.subject: Diana Taurasi
facts.fact: Diana Taurasi won five WNBA scoring titles (2006, 2008-2011), all with the Phoenix Mercury, and retired with a record 1,447 career three-pointers.
facts.volatileNote: Most-scoring-titles and career-threes marks are chaseable by active players.

facts.subject: Sue Bird
facts.fact: Sue Bird retired in 2022 as the WNBA's career leader in assists (3,234) and games played (580), all with the Seattle Storm.
facts.volatileNote: Career assists and games-played marks can be passed by active players.

facts.subject: Sabrina Ionescu
facts.fact: Sabrina Ionescu scored 37 of a possible 40 points in the final round of the 2023 WNBA All-Star three-point contest, a record higher than any NBA or WNBA contest round to that point.
facts.volatileNote: Contest scoring records can be broken.

facts.subject: 2023 Las Vegas Aces
facts.fact: The 2023 Las Vegas Aces went a then-record 34-6 and beat the New York Liberty 3-1 to repeat as champions — the WNBA's first back-to-back titlist since the 2001-02 Los Angeles Sparks. A'ja Wilson was Finals MVP.

facts.subject: Candace Parker
facts.fact: Candace Parker became the first player to win WNBA championships with three different franchises: the Los Angeles Sparks (2016), Chicago Sky (2021) and Las Vegas Aces (2023).

facts.subject: Jewell Loyd
facts.fact: Jewell Loyd scored 939 points for the Seattle Storm in 2023, then a WNBA single-season record, before A'ja Wilson passed her the following year.

facts.subject: Caitlin Clark
facts.fact: Iowa guard Caitlin Clark was the No. 1 overall pick of the 2024 WNBA draft, taken by the Indiana Fever, and won Rookie of the Year that season.

facts.subject: Caitlin Clark
facts.fact: As a 2024 rookie Caitlin Clark set the WNBA single-season assists record with 337, plus rookie records of 769 points and 122 three-pointers.
facts.volatileNote: Her 337-assist mark was passed by Alyssa Thomas (357) in 2025; rookie records remain chaseable.

facts.subject: Caitlin Clark
facts.fact: Caitlin Clark set the WNBA single-game assists record with 19 for Indiana at Dallas on July 17, 2024, breaking Courtney Vandersloot's mark of 18 set in 2020.
facts.volatileNote: Single-game record that could be broken.

facts.subject: Caitlin Clark
facts.fact: On July 6, 2024 Caitlin Clark became the first rookie in WNBA history to record a triple-double, going for 19 points, 12 rebounds and 13 assists in a win over the New York Liberty.

facts.subject: Angel Reese
facts.fact: As a rookie in 2024 Angel Reese recorded 15 consecutive double-doubles, breaking Candace Parker's WNBA record of 12.
facts.volatileNote: A streak record that could be extended or broken.

facts.subject: Angel Reese
facts.fact: In 2024 Angel Reese became the only player in WNBA history with three consecutive 20-rebound games, and she averaged 13.1 rebounds per game — no player had ever averaged more than 12.
facts.volatileNote: Could be matched or broken.

facts.subject: A'ja Wilson
facts.fact: A'ja Wilson scored 1,021 points in 2024, becoming the first WNBA player to reach 1,000 points in a single season, and averaged a record 26.9 per game.
facts.volatileNote: Single-season scoring records can be broken as schedules lengthen.

facts.subject: A'ja Wilson
facts.fact: A'ja Wilson set the WNBA single-season rebounding record with 451 in 2024, passing rookie Angel Reese's 446; the previous record had been Sylvia Fowles's 404.
facts.volatileNote: Single-season rebounding record can be broken.

facts.subject: A'ja Wilson
facts.fact: A'ja Wilson was a unanimous WNBA MVP in 2024, taking all 67 first-place votes.

facts.subject: A'ja Wilson
facts.fact: A'ja Wilson has won four WNBA MVP awards (2020, 2022, 2024, 2025), the most in league history; Sheryl Swoopes, Lisa Leslie and Lauren Jackson each won three.
facts.volatileNote: Wilson is active and can add more MVPs.

facts.subject: 2024 New York Liberty
facts.fact: The New York Liberty won their first WNBA championship in 2024 in their 28th season, beating the Minnesota Lynx 67-62 in overtime in Game 5 — the first winner-take-all Finals game to go to overtime. Jonquel Jones was Finals MVP.

facts.subject: USA women's basketball
facts.fact: At the 2024 Paris Olympics the U.S. women's basketball team beat France 67-66 for its eighth consecutive gold medal, the first team in any sport to win eight straight Olympic golds.
facts.volatileNote: The streak continues or ends at future Olympics.

facts.subject: Diana Taurasi
facts.fact: With gold at Paris 2024, Diana Taurasi became the first athlete in any team sport to win six Olympic gold medals (2004, 2008, 2012, 2016, 2020, 2024).
facts.volatileNote: Another athlete could match or pass six.

facts.subject: Golden State Valkyries
facts.fact: The Golden State Valkyries debuted in 2025 as the WNBA's first expansion team since 2008, went 23-21 and became the first WNBA franchise to reach the playoffs in its inaugural season; coach Natalie Nakase won Coach of the Year.

facts.subject: 2025 WNBA Finals
facts.fact: The 2025 WNBA Finals were the first played as a best-of-seven series; the Las Vegas Aces swept the Phoenix Mercury 4-0 on October 10, 2025 for their third title in four years, with A'ja Wilson named Finals MVP.

facts.subject: Napheesa Collier
facts.fact: Napheesa Collier averaged 22.9 points in 2025 on 53.1/40.3/90.6 shooting, becoming the second WNBA player to join the 50/40/90 club and the first to do it while averaging over 20 points.

facts.subject: Paige Bueckers
facts.fact: UConn's Paige Bueckers was the No. 1 overall pick of the 2025 WNBA draft, taken by the Dallas Wings, and won Rookie of the Year that season.

facts.subject: 2025 Defensive Player of the Year
facts.fact: Minnesota's Alanna Smith and Las Vegas's A'ja Wilson tied at 29 votes each to share the 2025 WNBA Defensive Player of the Year award, the first time the award was shared.

facts.subject: 2025 Minnesota Lynx
facts.fact: The 2025 Minnesota Lynx went 34-10 in a 44-game season, tying the 2023 Las Vegas Aces for the most regular-season wins in WNBA history, but lost the semifinals to Phoenix.
facts.volatileNote: Most-wins mark rises as the schedule lengthens.

facts.subject: 2026 WNBA expansion
facts.fact: The Toronto Tempo and Portland Fire joined the WNBA for the 2026 season, taking the league to 15 teams. Toronto is the WNBA's first franchise based outside the United States.

facts.subject: Azzi Fudd
facts.fact: UConn guard Azzi Fudd was the No. 1 overall pick of the 2026 WNBA draft, taken by the Dallas Wings — the second straight year Dallas held the top pick, reuniting Fudd with Paige Bueckers. Fudd is UConn's seventh No. 1 overall pick.

facts.subject: Marina Mabrey
facts.fact: Toronto Tempo guard Marina Mabrey scored 53 points with nine three-pointers against the Los Angeles Sparks on June 25, 2026, tying the WNBA single-game scoring record shared by Liz Cambage and A'ja Wilson.

facts.subject: Connecticut Sun
facts.fact: The Connecticut Sun are playing their final season in Uncasville in 2026 before relocating to Houston in 2027 and reviving the Comets name under Rockets owner Tilman Fertitta.
facts.volatileNote: Relocation plans can change before the 2027 season.

facts.subject: WNBA expansion plan
facts.fact: The WNBA has approved expansion franchises for Cleveland (2028), Detroit (2029) and Philadelphia (2030), which would take the league to 18 teams.
facts.volatileNote: Timelines and cities can shift before launch.

facts.subject: Alyssa Thomas
facts.fact: Alyssa Thomas is the WNBA's career triple-double leader and in 2025 became the first player in league history to record three consecutive triple-doubles; she also set the single-season assists record with 357 in 2025.
facts.volatileNote: Thomas is active; her triple-double and assist totals keep climbing.

facts.subject: WNBA leadership
facts.fact: Val Ackerman was the WNBA's first president (1996-2005), followed by Donna Orender, Laurel Richie and Lisa Borders. Cathy Engelbert became the league's first commissioner in July 2019, when the title was changed from president.

facts.subject: Defunct WNBA teams
facts.fact: Six WNBA franchises have folded: the Miami Sol and Portland Fire (after 2002), Cleveland Rockers (after 2003), Charlotte Sting (after 2006), Houston Comets (December 2008) and Sacramento Monarchs (2009).

facts.subject: Teresa Weatherspoon
facts.fact: New York Liberty guard Teresa Weatherspoon won the WNBA's first two Defensive Player of the Year awards, in 1997 and 1998.

facts.subject: Debbie Black
facts.fact: Debbie Black won the 2001 WNBA Defensive Player of the Year award playing for the Miami Sol, a franchise that folded after the following season.

facts.subject: Breanna Stewart
facts.fact: Breanna Stewart won Finals MVP for the Seattle Storm in both 2018 and 2020, each time as Seattle swept the Finals 3-0. She won regular-season MVP with Seattle in 2018 and with the New York Liberty in 2023.

facts.subject: Tina Charles
facts.fact: Tina Charles is the WNBA's all-time leading rebounder with 4,262, ahead of Sylvia Fowles (4,006), and is second all-time in career points.
facts.volatileNote: Charles has remained active; her totals and the leaderboard keep changing.

facts.subject: Becky Hammon
facts.fact: Becky Hammon, hired December 31, 2021, has coached the Las Vegas Aces to three WNBA championships (2022, 2023, 2025).
facts.volatileNote: Hammon is an active coach and can add titles.

facts.subject: WNBA coaching wins record
facts.fact: Mike Thibault set the WNBA record with 379 career regular-season coaching wins across the Connecticut Sun and Washington Mystics (2003-2022); Minnesota's Cheryl Reeve tied that mark in June 2026.
facts.volatileNote: Reeve is active and passing Thibault; the record total changes with every win.

facts.subject: Bill Laimbeer
facts.fact: Bill Laimbeer coached the Detroit Shock to three WNBA championships, in 2003, 2006 and 2008.

facts.subject: Aliyah Boston
facts.fact: South Carolina's Aliyah Boston was the No. 1 overall pick of the 2023 WNBA draft by the Indiana Fever and was a unanimous Rookie of the Year.

facts.subject: UConn
facts.fact: Connecticut has produced more No. 1 overall WNBA draft picks than any other school with seven: Sue Bird (2002), Diana Taurasi (2004), Tina Charles (2010), Maya Moore (2011), Breanna Stewart (2016), Paige Bueckers (2025) and Azzi Fudd (2026).
facts.volatileNote: Count grows with future drafts.

facts.subject: A'ja Wilson
facts.fact: South Carolina's A'ja Wilson was the No. 1 overall pick of the 2018 WNBA draft, taken by the Las Vegas Aces in the franchise's first season in Las Vegas, and won Rookie of the Year.

facts.subject: Betty Lennox
facts.fact: Betty Lennox won 2004 Finals MVP for the Seattle Storm, four years after winning Rookie of the Year with the Minnesota Lynx in 2000.

facts.subject: Yolanda Griffith
facts.fact: Yolanda Griffith of the Sacramento Monarchs won both regular-season MVP and Defensive Player of the Year in 1999.

facts.subject: Maya Moore
facts.fact: Maya Moore stepped away from the WNBA in 2019 at age 29, after four titles and a 2014 MVP, to work on overturning Jonathan Irons's wrongful conviction. Irons was freed in July 2020 and they married nine days later; Moore formally retired in January 2023.

facts.subject: Tina Charles
facts.fact: Tina Charles won the 2012 WNBA MVP award with the Connecticut Sun, two years after being the 2010 No. 1 overall pick by the same franchise.

facts.subject: Armintie Price
facts.fact: Armintie Price of the Chicago Sky won the 2007 WNBA Rookie of the Year award.

facts.subject: 1972 Munich men's final
facts.fact: The Soviet Union beat the United States 51-50 in the 1972 Munich Olympic men's gold medal game, the first ever Olympic defeat for a U.S. men's basketball team.

facts.subject: USA Olympic win streak
facts.fact: Before losing the 1972 final, the United States men's Olympic basketball team had a perfect 63-0 record across all Olympic play since 1936.

facts.subject: 1972 final controversy
facts.fact: The final three seconds of the 1972 Olympic final were played three separate times after officials mishandled a Soviet timeout and the game clock.

facts.subject: R. William Jones
facts.fact: R. William Jones, then FIBA's secretary general, left the stands and ordered the clock reset to three seconds for the decisive final inbounds of the 1972 Olympic final, despite having no authority to intervene.

facts.subject: Alexander Belov
facts.fact: Alexander Belov caught Ivan Yedeshko's full-court inbounds pass and scored the winning layup for the Soviet Union in the 1972 Olympic final.

facts.subject: Sergei Belov
facts.fact: Sergei Belov led all scorers with 20 points in the 1972 Olympic gold medal game, which finished 51-50.

facts.subject: 1972 USA team
facts.fact: The 1972 U.S. men's team unanimously refused their silver medals, which remain unclaimed in a vault in Lausanne, Switzerland.

facts.subject: Cuba
facts.fact: Cuba won the bronze medal in men's basketball at the 1972 Munich Olympics, its only Olympic basketball medal.

facts.subject: 1936 Berlin tournament
facts.fact: Olympic basketball debuted at the 1936 Berlin Games on outdoor clay and dirt tennis courts; heavy rain in the final turned the court to mud and made dribbling nearly impossible.

facts.subject: 1936 gold medal game
facts.fact: The United States beat Canada 19-8 in the 1936 Olympic men's gold medal game, played in a downpour on a dirt court.

facts.subject: James Naismith
facts.fact: James Naismith, the inventor of basketball, presented the medals at the 1936 Berlin Olympics, the sport's Olympic debut.

facts.subject: Mexico
facts.fact: Mexico won the bronze medal in men's basketball at the 1936 Berlin Olympics, the nation's only Olympic basketball medal.

facts.subject: USA men's Olympic record
facts.fact: The United States men's team has won 17 Olympic gold medals in 20 tournaments entered, with one silver (1972) and two bronzes (1988, 2004).
facts.volatileNote: Total increases if the USA wins gold at future Olympics (LA 2028 onward).

facts.subject: Yugoslavia 1980
facts.fact: Yugoslavia won the men's Olympic gold medal at the 1980 Moscow Games, beating Italy in the final, in a tournament the United States boycotted.

facts.subject: Soviet Union 1988
facts.fact: The Soviet Union won men's basketball gold at the 1988 Seoul Olympics, beating the United States in the semifinal and Yugoslavia in the final; the U.S. took bronze.

facts.subject: Lithuania 1992
facts.fact: Lithuania beat the Unified Team (the former Soviet republics) 82-78 in the 1992 Barcelona bronze medal game, its first medal as an independent nation.

facts.subject: Lithuania tie-dye uniforms
facts.fact: The Grateful Dead helped fund newly independent Lithuania's 1992 Olympic basketball team, which collected its bronze medals wearing tie-dye shirts featuring a slam-dunking skeleton.

facts.subject: Lithuania medal run
facts.fact: Lithuania won the men's Olympic bronze medal at three consecutive Games: 1992, 1996 and 2000.

facts.subject: 2000 Sydney semifinal
facts.fact: The United States survived Lithuania 85-83 in the 2000 Sydney semifinal when Sarunas Jasikevicius's last-second three-pointer was an air ball; it was the closest game an NBA-era U.S. Olympic team had played to that point.

facts.subject: Argentina 2004
facts.fact: Argentina won the 2004 Athens men's Olympic gold medal, beating the United States 89-81 in the semifinal and Italy 84-69 in the final.

facts.subject: 2004 USA team
facts.fact: The 2004 U.S. men's Olympic team lost three games — to Puerto Rico, Lithuania and Argentina — the most ever by a U.S. men's Olympic squad, and settled for bronze under coach Larry Brown.

facts.subject: Puerto Rico upset
facts.fact: Puerto Rico beat the United States 92-73 in the 2004 Olympic opener, the largest margin of defeat ever suffered by a U.S. men's Olympic team.

facts.subject: Manu Ginobili
facts.fact: Manu Ginobili was named MVP of the 2004 Athens Olympic men's basketball tournament after leading Argentina to gold.

facts.subject: 2008 Redeem Team
facts.fact: The 2008 'Redeem Team' went 8-0 and beat Spain 118-107 in the Beijing gold medal game, coached by Mike Krzyzewski with Jerry Colangelo as managing director.

facts.subject: 2012 London final
facts.fact: The United States beat Spain 107-100 in the 2012 London men's gold medal game, Spain's second straight Olympic final loss to the Americans.

facts.subject: 2016 Rio bronze game
facts.fact: Spain edged Australia 89-88 for the men's bronze medal at the 2016 Rio Olympics; Serbia took silver.

facts.subject: Australia Boomers
facts.fact: Australia won its first ever Olympic men's basketball medal at the delayed 2020 Tokyo Games, beating Slovenia 107-93 in the bronze medal game.

facts.subject: Patty Mills
facts.fact: Patty Mills scored 42 points with nine assists in Australia's 2020 Tokyo bronze medal win over Slovenia, the second-highest Olympic scoring game by an Australian after Eddie Palubinskas's 48 in 1976.

facts.subject: 2024 Paris final
facts.fact: The United States beat France 98-87 in the 2024 Paris men's gold medal game for a fifth consecutive Olympic title; LeBron James was named tournament MVP.

facts.subject: Stephen Curry
facts.fact: Stephen Curry scored 36 points with 10 assists in the United States' 95-91 semifinal comeback win over Serbia at the 2024 Paris Olympics.

facts.subject: Giannis Antetokounmpo
facts.fact: Giannis Antetokounmpo led the 2024 Paris Olympic men's tournament in scoring at 25.8 points per game for Greece.

facts.subject: Victor Wembanyama
facts.fact: Victor Wembanyama scored 26 points with 8 rebounds for France in the 2024 Paris Olympic gold medal game loss to the United States.

facts.subject: Christian Laettner
facts.fact: Christian Laettner of Duke was the only college player on the 1992 Dream Team, chosen over LSU's Shaquille O'Neal.

facts.subject: Chuck Daly
facts.fact: Chuck Daly, who had just coached the Detroit Pistons to back-to-back NBA titles, was the head coach of the 1992 Dream Team.

facts.subject: 1992 opener vs Angola
facts.fact: The Dream Team's first Olympic game was a 116-48 win over Angola at the 1992 Barcelona Games.

facts.subject: 1992 dominance
facts.fact: The 1992 Dream Team went 8-0 with an average margin of victory of 43.8 points.

facts.subject: 1992 gold medal game
facts.fact: The Dream Team's closest game of the 1992 Olympics was the 117-85 gold medal win over Croatia, a 32-point margin.

facts.subject: Isiah Thomas
facts.fact: Isiah Thomas, a two-time NBA champion point guard with Detroit, was famously left off the 1992 Dream Team roster.

facts.subject: Drazen Petrovic
facts.fact: Drazen Petrovic led all scorers with 24 points for Croatia in the 1992 Olympic gold medal game against the Dream Team.

facts.subject: 1950 World Championship
facts.fact: The first FIBA World Championship was held in Argentina in 1950, and the host nation won it, beating the United States.

facts.subject: All-time World Cup titles
facts.fact: The United States and Yugoslavia are tied for the most FIBA World Cup titles with five each.
facts.volatileNote: The USA can add titles at future World Cups; Yugoslavia no longer exists so its total is fixed.

facts.subject: Rolando Frazer
facts.fact: Rolando Frazer of Panama was named MVP of the 1982 FIBA World Championship in Colombia.

facts.subject: Drazen Petrovic
facts.fact: Drazen Petrovic was named MVP of the 1986 FIBA World Championship in Spain, which the United States won.

facts.subject: Toni Kukoc
facts.fact: Toni Kukoc was named MVP of the 1990 FIBA World Championship in Argentina, won by Yugoslavia.

facts.subject: Shaquille O'Neal
facts.fact: Shaquille O'Neal was MVP of the 1994 FIBA World Championship in Canada, where the U.S. 'Dream Team II' beat Russia 137-91 in the final.

facts.subject: Dejan Bodiroga
facts.fact: Dejan Bodiroga was MVP of the 1998 FIBA World Championship in Greece, where FR Yugoslavia beat Russia 64-62 in the final.

facts.subject: 2002 World Championship final
facts.fact: Yugoslavia beat Argentina 84-77 in overtime in the 2002 FIBA World Championship final in Indianapolis, with Dejan Bodiroga scoring 27 points.

facts.subject: Dirk Nowitzki
facts.fact: Dirk Nowitzki was named MVP of the 2002 FIBA World Championship, leading all scorers at 24.0 points per game while Germany finished third.

facts.subject: 2002 USA team
facts.fact: The United States finished sixth at the 2002 FIBA World Championship on home soil in Indianapolis, losing to Argentina in the group stage and to Yugoslavia in the quarterfinals.

facts.subject: Spain 2006
facts.fact: Spain won its first FIBA World Championship in 2006 in Japan, going 9-0 and beating Greece 70-47 in the final; Pau Gasol was MVP.

facts.subject: Greece over USA 2006
facts.fact: Greece beat the United States 101-95 in the semifinal of the 2006 FIBA World Championship.

facts.subject: Kevin Durant
facts.fact: Kevin Durant was MVP of the 2010 FIBA World Championship in Turkey, averaging 22.8 points as the United States beat host Turkey 81-64 in the final.

facts.subject: Kyrie Irving
facts.fact: Kyrie Irving was MVP of the 2014 FIBA World Cup in Spain, where the United States beat Serbia 129-92 in the final.

facts.subject: Ricky Rubio
facts.fact: Ricky Rubio was MVP of the 2019 FIBA World Cup in China, where Spain beat Argentina 95-75 in the final for its second world title.

facts.subject: 2019 USA team
facts.fact: The United States finished seventh at the 2019 FIBA World Cup, its worst ever World Cup result, after losing to France in the quarterfinals.

facts.subject: Germany 2023
facts.fact: Germany went 8-0 to win its first FIBA World Cup in 2023, beating Serbia 83-77 in the final; captain Dennis Schroder was named MVP.

facts.subject: 2023 semifinal
facts.fact: Germany beat the United States 113-111 in the 2023 FIBA World Cup semifinal, with Andreas Obst scoring 24 points.

facts.subject: Canada 2023
facts.fact: Canada won its first ever FIBA World Cup medal in 2023, beating the United States 127-118 in overtime in the bronze medal game.

facts.subject: 1935 EuroBasket
facts.fact: The first EuroBasket was held in Switzerland in 1935 and was won by Latvia, which beat Spain in the final.

facts.subject: Lithuania pre-war titles
facts.fact: Lithuania won the last two EuroBaskets before World War II, in 1937 and 1939, and did not win a third until 2003.

facts.subject: Soviet Union EuroBasket record
facts.fact: The Soviet Union won a record 14 EuroBasket titles, far ahead of Yugoslavia's eight.

facts.subject: EuroBasket 1987 final
facts.fact: Greece beat the Soviet Union 103-101 in overtime in the EuroBasket 1987 final in Athens for its first major title, behind 40 points from Nikos Galis.

facts.subject: Nikos Galis
facts.fact: Nikos Galis was both MVP and leading scorer of EuroBasket 1987, piling up 296 points in eight games.

facts.subject: Germany 1993
facts.fact: Germany won its first EuroBasket title in 1993 on home soil, beating Russia 71-70 in the final.

facts.subject: Sarunas Jasikevicius
facts.fact: Lithuania won EuroBasket 2003 in Sweden and Sarunas Jasikevicius was named MVP, averaging 14.0 points and 8.2 assists.

facts.subject: Pau Gasol
facts.fact: Pau Gasol won EuroBasket MVP twice, in 2009 and 2015, sharing the record for most EuroBasket MVP awards with Kresimir Cosic.

facts.subject: Slovenia 2017
facts.fact: Slovenia won its first EuroBasket title in 2017, beating Serbia 93-85 in the final; Goran Dragic was named tournament MVP.

facts.subject: Germany 2025
facts.fact: Germany won EuroBasket 2025, beating Turkey 88-83 in the final, with Dennis Schroder named MVP and Greece taking bronze.
facts.volatileNote: Germany are the reigning European champions only until the next EuroBasket is played.

facts.subject: Real Madrid
facts.fact: Real Madrid has won a record 11 EuroLeague/European Cup titles, ahead of CSKA Moscow's eight and Panathinaikos's seven.
facts.volatileNote: Counts change whenever any of these clubs wins another EuroLeague.

facts.subject: 2026 EuroLeague Final Four
facts.fact: Olympiacos beat Real Madrid 92-85 to win the 2026 EuroLeague title, its fourth overall and first since 2013; Evan Fournier was named Final Four MVP.
facts.volatileNote: Reigning champion changes each season.

facts.subject: Luka Doncic
facts.fact: Luka Doncic won both the EuroLeague MVP and the Final Four MVP in 2018 with Real Madrid at age 19, becoming the youngest EuroLeague MVP ever.

facts.subject: Jugoplastika Split
facts.fact: Jugoplastika Split (later POP 84) won three consecutive European Cup titles in 1989, 1990 and 1991 with Toni Kukoc and Dino Radja.

facts.subject: Toni Kukoc
facts.fact: Toni Kukoc won the EuroLeague Final Four MVP award three times (1990, 1991, 1993); only Vassilis Spanoulis has matched that total.

facts.subject: Manu Ginobili
facts.fact: Manu Ginobili won the 2001 EuroLeague title and Finals MVP with Kinder Bologna before joining the San Antonio Spurs.

facts.subject: Sarunas Jasikevicius
facts.fact: Sarunas Jasikevicius won four EuroLeague titles as a player: with FC Barcelona in 2003, Maccabi Tel Aviv in 2004 and 2005, and Panathinaikos in 2009.

facts.subject: Drazen Petrovic
facts.fact: Playing for Cibona on 5 October 1985, Drazen Petrovic scored 112 points in a Yugoslav league game against Olimpija Ljubljana, including 67 in the first half and 22-of-22 from the free throw line.

facts.subject: Drazen Petrovic
facts.fact: Drazen Petrovic was drafted 60th overall in the third round of the 1986 NBA draft by the Portland Trail Blazers, and did not join the NBA until 1989.

facts.subject: Drazen Petrovic
facts.fact: Drazen Petrovic died in a car crash on the German autobahn on 7 June 1993 at age 28, having just averaged a career-high 22.3 points per game for the New Jersey Nets; he was inducted into the Naismith Hall of Fame in 2002.

facts.subject: Arvydas Sabonis
facts.fact: Arvydas Sabonis was drafted by Atlanta in 1985 (a pick voided because he was under 21) and then by Portland 24th overall in 1986, but did not make his NBA debut until 1995 at age 30.

facts.subject: Arvydas Sabonis
facts.fact: Arvydas Sabonis won Olympic gold with the Soviet Union in 1988, then bronze medals with independent Lithuania in 1992 and 1996.

facts.subject: Oscar Schmidt
facts.fact: Brazil's Oscar Schmidt is the all-time leading scorer in Olympic basketball history with 1,093 points across five Games.

facts.subject: Oscar Schmidt
facts.fact: Oscar Schmidt scored 46 points as Brazil beat the United States 120-115 in the 1987 Pan American Games gold medal game in Indianapolis.

facts.subject: Oscar Schmidt
facts.fact: Oscar Schmidt was drafted 131st overall by the New Jersey Nets in 1984 but never played in the NBA, turning down their offer to keep playing in Italy and for Brazil's national team; he was inducted into the Hall of Fame in 2013.

facts.subject: Oscar Schmidt
facts.fact: Oscar Schmidt's nickname was 'Mao Santa' — Portuguese for 'Holy Hand'.

facts.subject: Sergei Belov
facts.fact: Sergei Belov became the first international player inducted into the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame, in 1992, and lit the Olympic cauldron at the 1980 Moscow Games.

facts.subject: Kresimir Cosic
facts.fact: Yugoslavia's Kresimir Cosic played college basketball at Brigham Young University from 1970 to 1973, and won Olympic gold in 1980 plus silvers in 1968 and 1976.

facts.subject: Toni Kukoc
facts.fact: Toni Kukoc was drafted 29th overall in the second round of the 1990 NBA draft by the Chicago Bulls, and won Olympic silver with Yugoslavia in 1988 and with Croatia in 1992.

facts.subject: Giannis Antetokounmpo
facts.fact: Giannis Antetokounmpo was born in Athens, Greece on 6 December 1994 to Nigerian parents from Lagos, and received Greek citizenship on 9 May 2013, weeks before being drafted 15th overall by the Milwaukee Bucks.

facts.subject: Giannis Antetokounmpo
facts.fact: Giannis Antetokounmpo led EuroBasket 2022 in scoring at 29.3 points per game and made the All-Tournament Team.

facts.subject: Nikola Jokic
facts.fact: Nikola Jokic was drafted 41st overall by the Denver Nuggets in 2014, an announcement that aired on ESPN alongside a Taco Bell commercial; he is the lowest-drafted player ever to win NBA MVP.

facts.subject: Nikola Jokic
facts.fact: Nikola Jokic won an Olympic silver medal with Serbia in 2016 and a bronze in 2024.

facts.subject: Yao Ming
facts.fact: Yao Ming was the first overall pick of the 2002 NBA draft by the Houston Rockets, coming from the Shanghai Sharks whom he had just led to a CBA title; he was China's flag bearer at the 2004 and 2008 Olympic opening ceremonies.

facts.subject: Yao Ming
facts.fact: Yao Ming, listed at 7 feet 6 inches, became the first Chinese national inducted into the Naismith Hall of Fame in 2016, in the same class as Shaquille O'Neal and Allen Iverson.

facts.subject: Spain
facts.fact: Spain's golden generation won World Cups in 2006 and 2019, EuroBaskets in 2009, 2011, 2015 and 2022, and Olympic silver in 2008 and 2012.

facts.subject: 2008 Beijing final
facts.fact: The United States beat Spain 118-107 in the 2008 Beijing Olympic men's final, the closest gold medal game of the NBA era to that point.

facts.subject: Angola
facts.fact: Angola has won 12 AfroBasket titles, by far the most of any nation, most recently in 2025.
facts.volatileNote: Total rises if Angola wins another AfroBasket.

facts.subject: Nigeria
facts.fact: Nigeria beat the United States 90-87 in a July 2021 Las Vegas exhibition, becoming the first African nation ever to beat a U.S. men's national team.

facts.subject: 1976 Montreal
facts.fact: Women's basketball debuted at the 1976 Montreal Olympics and the Soviet Union won the gold medal, ahead of the United States and Bulgaria.

facts.subject: USA women's dynasty
facts.fact: The United States women have won eight consecutive Olympic gold medals, from 1996 Atlanta through 2024 Paris.
facts.volatileNote: Streak extends or ends at LA 2028.

facts.subject: 2024 Paris women's final
facts.fact: The United States beat France 67-66 in the 2024 Paris women's gold medal game; A'ja Wilson had 21 points and 13 rebounds and was named tournament MVP.

facts.subject: Diana Taurasi
