facts.fact: Diana Taurasi won a record six Olympic gold medals in basketball (2004, 2008, 2012, 2016, 2020 and 2024), breaking a tie with Sue Bird's five.
facts.volatileNote: Another player could match or pass six golds at future Games.

facts.subject: 2024 Paris women's bronze
facts.fact: Australia beat Belgium 85-81 for the women's bronze medal at the 2024 Paris Olympics.

facts.subject: Brazil 1994
facts.fact: Brazil won the 1994 Women's World Championship in Australia, beating China 96-87 in the final, with Hortencia Marcari leading the tournament in scoring at 27.6 points per game.

facts.subject: Australia 2006
facts.fact: Australia won its first Women's World Championship gold in 2006 in Brazil, captained by Lauren Jackson, who averaged 21.3 points and 8.9 rebounds.

facts.subject: USA women's World Cup record
facts.fact: The United States has won 11 Women's Basketball World Cup gold medals, ahead of the Soviet Union's six.
facts.volatileNote: Total can grow at each Women's World Cup, including the 2026 edition in Germany.

facts.subject: Lauren Jackson
facts.fact: Lauren Jackson won five Olympic medals for Australia — silver in 2000, 2004 and 2008 and bronze in 2012 and 2024 — but never won Olympic gold.

facts.subject: Lauren Jackson
facts.fact: Lauren Jackson was the first overall pick of the 2001 WNBA draft by the Seattle Storm and went on to win WNBA MVP in 2003, 2007 and 2010.

facts.subject: Lauren Jackson
facts.fact: Lauren Jackson returned to the Australian national team for the 2022 Women's World Cup in Sydney at age 41, scoring 30 points against Canada as Australia won bronze.

facts.subject: Argentina
facts.fact: Argentina's 2004 Athens gold is the only Olympic men's basketball title won by a nation other than the United States, the Soviet Union or Yugoslavia.

facts.subject: Manu Ginobili
facts.fact: Manu Ginobili was drafted 57th overall in the second round of the 1999 NBA draft by the San Antonio Spurs and was inducted into the Naismith Hall of Fame in 2022 on the first ballot.

facts.subject: Slovenia
facts.fact: Despite Luka Doncic, Slovenia failed to qualify for the 2024 Paris Olympics, losing in the Olympic Qualifying Tournament.

facts.subject: Yugoslavia MVPs
facts.fact: Yugoslavia has produced the most FIBA World Cup MVPs, with Ivo Daneu (1967), Dragan Kicanovic (1974), Drazen Dalipagic (1978), Drazen Petrovic (1986) and Toni Kukoc (1990).

facts.subject: Holcombe Rucker
facts.fact: Holcombe Rucker, a New York City teacher and playground director, founded what is believed to be New York City's first annual summer basketball tournament in 1950; it expanded in 1953 to include high school and college-aged players.

facts.subject: Rucker Park
facts.fact: The Harlem court universally called 'Rucker Park' is officially named Greg Marius Court at Holcombe Rucker Park, located at 155th Street and Frederick Douglass Boulevard in Manhattan.

facts.subject: Holcombe Rucker
facts.fact: Holcombe Rucker died in 1965; he had secured over 700 athletic scholarships for players who came through his program, and afterward his proteges Bob McCullough and Freddie Crawford established the Rucker Pro League.

facts.subject: Entertainers Basketball Classic
facts.fact: Greg Marius founded the Entertainer's Basketball Classic (EBC) at Rucker Park in 1982, reviving the tournament after quiet years in the 1970s; the event took the EBC name in 1986.

facts.subject: Earl Manigault
facts.fact: Earl Manigault, nicknamed 'The Goat', was a 6-foot-1 guard born September 7, 1944 in Charleston, South Carolina; he died May 15, 1998 of congestive heart failure and never played professionally.

facts.subject: Earl Manigault
facts.fact: Earl 'The Goat' Manigault reportedly reverse dunked 36 times in a row to win a $60 bet.

facts.subject: Earl Manigault
facts.fact: Kareem Abdul-Jabbar called Earl 'The Goat' Manigault 'the best basketball player his size in the history of New York City'.

facts.subject: Earl Manigault
facts.fact: The 1996 HBO film 'Rebound: The Legend of Earl "The Goat" Manigault' starred Don Cheadle as Manigault.

facts.subject: Earl Manigault
facts.fact: Earl Manigault's entire college career was one semester at Johnson C. Smith University in 1964; he later tried out for the ABA's Utah Stars but did not make the team.

facts.subject: Earl Manigault
facts.fact: Earl Manigault averaged 24 points and 11 rebounds per game at Benjamin Franklin High School in Manhattan, then 31 points and 13 rebounds per game at Laurinburg Institute in North Carolina.

facts.subject: Joe Hammond
facts.fact: Joe Hammond of Harlem, nicknamed 'The Destroyer', once scored 50 points in a half against Julius Erving at Rucker Park; The New York Times in 1990 described him as the best streetball player ever.

facts.subject: Joe Hammond
facts.fact: The Los Angeles Lakers selected Joe 'The Destroyer' Hammond with the fifth pick of the 1971 NBA hardship (early entry) draft; Hammond turned the opportunity down and never played in the NBA.

facts.subject: Joe Hammond
facts.fact: Joe Hammond, listed at 6 feet 4 inches, dropped out of William Howard Taft High School in the Bronx in the ninth grade; he later won an Eastern Professional Basketball League title with the Allentown Jets in 1970.

facts.subject: Pee Wee Kirkland
facts.fact: Richard 'Pee Wee' Kirkland was selected by the Chicago Bulls in the 13th round (172nd overall) of the 1969 NBA draft but never played in the league; he was arrested in 1971 and served time for conspiracy to sell narcotics and tax evasion.

facts.subject: Pee Wee Kirkland
facts.fact: Pee Wee Kirkland averaged 41 points per game at Kittrell College, a junior college in North Carolina, during the 1963-64 season.

facts.subject: Pee Wee Kirkland
facts.fact: At Norfolk State, Pee Wee Kirkland played alongside future NBA champion Bob Dandridge; the Spartans went 25-2 and won the 1968 CIAA title.

facts.subject: Herman Knowings
facts.fact: Herman Knowings, a Rucker Park star of the 1960s and 1970s out of Benjamin Franklin High School in Harlem, was nicknamed 'The Helicopter' for his hang time and shot-blocking.

facts.subject: Connie Hawkins
facts.fact: Connie 'The Hawk' Hawkins won the first ABA MVP award in 1968, averaging 26.8 points, and led the Pittsburgh Pipers to the first ABA championship; he was also playoffs MVP.

facts.subject: Connie Hawkins
facts.fact: Wrongly implicated in the 1961 college point-shaving scandal and never charged, Connie Hawkins was formally banned from the NBA in 1966; he filed an antitrust lawsuit and the league settled after the 1968-69 season, admitting him and paying nearly $1.3 million.

facts.subject: Connie Hawkins
facts.fact: Connie Hawkins spent four years with the Harlem Globetrotters (1963-1967) before the ABA and NBA; in his first NBA season (1969-70) with the Phoenix Suns he averaged 24.6 points, 10.4 rebounds and 4.8 assists.

facts.subject: Fly Williams
facts.fact: James 'Fly' Williams of Brownsville, Brooklyn inspired the Austin Peay State University chant 'The Fly is open, let's go Peay!'; his No. 35 was retired by the school on February 5, 2009.

facts.subject: Fly Williams
facts.fact: Fly Williams averaged 29.4 points per game as a freshman at Austin Peay and was taken second overall in the 1974 ABA draft by the Denver Nuggets, who sold his contract to the Spirits of St. Louis.

facts.subject: Lloyd Daniels
facts.fact: Lloyd Daniels, born September 4, 1967, was nicknamed 'Swee'Pea' after the Popeye cartoon character; he was shot twice in a drug-related shooting on May 11, 1989 and did not reach the NBA until signing with the San Antonio Spurs in 1992.

facts.subject: Demetrius Mitchell
facts.fact: Demetrius 'Hook' Mitchell, a 5-foot-10 Oakland playground legend who grew up with Jason Kidd and Gary Payton, was known for dunking over a parked Honda Accord and was the subject of the 2003 documentary 'Hooked'.

facts.subject: God Shammgod
facts.fact: God Shammgod, born April 29, 1976, starred at Providence College and gave his name to 'the Shammgod' crossover dribble; he was drafted 46th overall in 1997 by Washington and played just 20 NBA games.

facts.subject: West 4th Street Courts
facts.fact: The West Fourth Street Courts in Greenwich Village, Manhattan are nicknamed 'The Cage'; the court is famously smaller than regulation size, which produces extremely physical play.

facts.subject: West 4th Street Courts
facts.fact: The West 4th Street summer league was founded by a limousine driver named Kenny Graham; officials estimate the league draws more than 100,000 spectators each summer, and Anthony Mason's Prime Time squad won five titles in the early 1990s.

facts.subject: Dyckman Basketball Tournament
facts.fact: The Dyckman Basketball Tournament was founded in 1990 by Kenneth Stevens, Omar Booth and Michael Jenkins at Monsignor Kett Playground in the Inwood/Washington Heights section of Manhattan, as a response to the crack epidemic.

facts.subject: Make it, take it
facts.fact: In streetball, 'make it, take it' (also called winner's ball) means the team that scores keeps possession instead of surrendering the ball to the opponent.

facts.subject: Streetball officiating
facts.fact: Pickup streetball is typically played without referees: players call their own fouls, free throws are usually not awarded, and a called foul simply gives possession to the fouled team.

facts.subject: AND1 Mixtape Vol. 1
facts.fact: The first AND1 mixtape, known as 'the Skip Tape', was built around grainy footage of Rafer 'Skip to My Lou' Alston and was circulated as a promotional VHS to camps, clinics and record labels; his high school coach Ron Naclerio helped get the tape to AND1.

facts.subject: Rafer Alston
facts.fact: Rafer Alston, born July 24, 1976 and known on the playground as 'Skip to My Lou', attended Benjamin N. Cardozo High School in Queens and played college ball at Ventura College, Fresno City College and Fresno State.

facts.subject: Rafer Alston
facts.fact: Rafer Alston was drafted in the second round, 39th overall, of the 1998 NBA draft by the Milwaukee Bucks, and later started for the Orlando Magic team that reached the 2009 NBA Finals.

facts.subject: AND1 Mixtape Tour
facts.fact: The AND1 Live/Mixtape Tour ran from 1998 to 2008 and its games were televised in half-hour 'Streetball' segments on ESPN2; AND1 released ten mixtape volumes, ending with AND1 Mixtape X in 2008.

facts.subject: Grayson Boucher
facts.fact: Grayson 'The Professor' Boucher, a 5-foot-10 guard from Keizer, Oregon who played at Chemeketa Community College, earned his AND1 roster spot at an Open Run tryout when the tour stopped in Portland, Oregon.

facts.subject: Grayson Boucher
facts.fact: Grayson Boucher appeared in seven seasons of the ESPN series 'Streetball', five AND1 mixtape DVDs, four commercials and an AND1 video game before leaving the tour in January 2011 to join Ball Up.

facts.subject: Troy Jackson
facts.fact: Troy 'Escalade' Jackson, the 6-foot-10 AND1 center from Queens, was the younger brother of NBA point guard Mark Jackson; he joined the tour in 2002 and died of hypertensive heart disease on February 20, 2011 at age 38.

facts.subject: Troy Jackson
facts.fact: Troy 'Escalade' Jackson played college basketball at the University of Louisville from 1996 to 1998, appearing in 20 games and averaging 3.0 points and 1.6 rebounds; he appeared on the cover of Sports Illustrated on June 13, 2005.

facts.subject: Philip Champion
facts.fact: AND1's most famous ballhandler, 'Hot Sauce', is Philip Champion, born June 13, 1976 at Fort Campbell, Kentucky and raised in Jacksonville, Florida; he turned pro in 2000 and appeared in the 2006 film 'Crossover'.

facts.subject: Larry Williams
facts.fact: AND1 tour star 'The Bone Collector' is Larry Williams of Tyler, Texas.

facts.subject: Waliyy Dixon
facts.fact: AND1 tour player 'Main Event' is Waliyy Dixon of Linden, New Jersey.

facts.subject: Aaron Owens
facts.fact: AND1 tour guard 'AO' is Aaron Owens of Philadelphia, Pennsylvania.

facts.subject: Anthony Heyward
facts.fact: AND1 tour player '1/2 Man 1/2 Amazing' is Anthony Heyward Jr. of Brooklyn, New York.

facts.subject: Taurian Fontenette
facts.fact: AND1 tour dunker 'The Air Up There' is Taurian Fontenette of Hitchcock, Texas; 'Alimoe / The Black Widow' was Tyrone Evans of Harlem.

facts.subject: Harlem Globetrotters
facts.fact: Despite the name, the Harlem Globetrotters were founded in 1926 at the Giles American Legion Post #87 on Chicago's South Side, evolving from the Savoy Big Five; they had no original connection to Harlem.

facts.subject: Harlem Globetrotters
facts.fact: The Harlem Globetrotters played their first game in the small town of Hinckley, Illinois.

facts.subject: Abe Saperstein
facts.fact: Abe Saperstein, founder, owner and first coach of the Harlem Globetrotters, was born in London, England on July 4, 1902 and died March 15, 1966; at 5 feet 3 inches he is the shortest male member of the Basketball Hall of Fame, inducted in 1971.

facts.subject: Abe Saperstein
facts.fact: Abe Saperstein founded the American Basketball League in 1961 and introduced the three-point shot to major professional basketball, setting the line at 25 feet.

facts.subject: Harlem Globetrotters
facts.fact: The Harlem Globetrotters' signature song is Brother Bones' whistled version of 'Sweet Georgia Brown'.

facts.subject: 1948 Globetrotters-Lakers game
facts.fact: On February 19, 1948 at Chicago Stadium, before 17,853 fans, the Harlem Globetrotters beat George Mikan's Minneapolis Lakers 61-59 on Ermer Robinson's one-handed shot from about 30 feet in the closing seconds.

facts.subject: 1949 Globetrotters-Lakers rematch
facts.fact: The Globetrotters beat the Minneapolis Lakers again a year after their famous 1948 upset, winning 49-45; the two teams then played six more games, all of which the Lakers won.

facts.subject: Harlem Globetrotters
facts.fact: The Harlem Globetrotters won the 1940 World Professional Basketball Tournament in Chicago, beating the Chicago Bruins 31-29 in the final.

facts.subject: Goose Tatum
facts.fact: Reece 'Goose' Tatum (May 31, 1921 - January 18, 1967) played for the Globetrotters from 1942 to 1955, stood 6-foot-4 with an arm span of roughly 84 inches, also played Negro League baseball for the Indianapolis Clowns, and was inducted into the Basketball Hall of Fame in 2011.

facts.subject: Harlem Magicians
facts.fact: After leaving the Globetrotters, Goose Tatum and Marques Haynes co-founded a rival touring team, the Harlem Magicians, in 1953.

facts.subject: Marques Haynes
facts.fact: Marques Haynes (March 10, 1926 - May 22, 2015), billed as the world's greatest dribbler, played for Langston University, was with the Globetrotters 1947-1953 and 1972-1979, played an estimated 12,000-plus games over a 46-year career, and entered the Basketball Hall of Fame in 1998.

facts.subject: Meadowlark Lemon
facts.fact: Meadow George 'Meadowlark' Lemon III (April 25, 1932 - December 27, 2015), the Globetrotters' 'Clown Prince', joined the team in 1955, played 22 years, wore No. 36, and was inducted into the Basketball Hall of Fame in 2003.

facts.subject: Curly Neal
facts.fact: Frederick 'Curly' Neal (May 19, 1942 - March 26, 2020) played 22 seasons for the Globetrotters (1963-1985), appeared in more than 6,000 games in 97 countries, and had his No. 22 retired at Madison Square Garden on February 15, 2008.

facts.subject: Globetrotters retired numbers
facts.fact: Globetrotters retired numbers include Wilt Chamberlain's No. 13, Marques Haynes' No. 20, Curly Neal's No. 22, Meadowlark Lemon's No. 36 and Goose Tatum's No. 50 (retired February 8, 2002).

facts.subject: Wilt Chamberlain
facts.fact: Wilt Chamberlain played the 1958-59 season with the Harlem Globetrotters for $50,000 because NBA rules barred players until their college class had graduated; the team retired his No. 13 on March 9, 2000.

facts.subject: Washington Generals
facts.fact: The Washington Generals, the Globetrotters' designated opponents, were created in 1952 by Louis 'Red' Klotz, a former player for the Philadelphia SPHAs.

facts.subject: Washington Generals
facts.fact: Playing under the name New Jersey Reds on January 5, 1971 in Martin, Tennessee, Red Klotz's team beat the Globetrotters 100-99 in overtime, with the 50-year-old Klotz hitting the winning basket in the final seconds.

facts.subject: Washington Generals
facts.fact: The Washington Generals have lost to the Harlem Globetrotters more than 16,000 times, winning somewhere between three and six games depending on the source.
facts.volatileNote: The Generals were revived in 2017 and keep touring, so the loss total continues to climb.

facts.subject: Lynette Woodard
facts.fact: In 1985 Lynette Woodard became the first woman ever to play for the Harlem Globetrotters; she had scored 3,649 points at Kansas and won Olympic gold in 1984, and her cousin Hubert 'Geese' Ausbie played for the Globetrotters from 1961 to 1985.

facts.subject: Harlem Globetrotters
facts.fact: The Harlem Globetrotters have played more than 26,000 exhibition games in 124 countries and territories.
facts.volatileNote: The team still tours, so the games-played and countries-visited totals keep rising.

facts.subject: Bob Douglas
facts.fact: Bob Douglas, born November 4, 1882 in Saint Kitts, British West Indies, founded the New York Renaissance in October 1923 and owned and coached the team through 1949; the Rens were the first fully all-Black, Black-owned professional basketball team.

facts.subject: New York Renaissance
facts.fact: The New York Rens took their name from and played their home games at the Renaissance Casino and Ballroom at 138th Street and Seventh Avenue in Harlem.

facts.subject: New York Renaissance
facts.fact: During the 1932-33 season the New York Rens won 88 consecutive games, a mark never matched by a professional basketball team; the team compiled a 2,588-529 record from 1923 to 1948.

facts.subject: New York Renaissance
facts.fact: The New York Rens won the inaugural 1939 World Professional Basketball Tournament in Chicago, beating the Oshkosh All-Stars 34-25 in the final.

facts.subject: New York Renaissance
facts.fact: The Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame inducted the 1932-33 New York Renaissance collectively as a team in 1963.

facts.subject: Dayton Rens
facts.fact: During the 1948-49 season the Rens relocated to Dayton, Ohio as the Dayton Rens to replace the folded Detroit Vagabond Kings in the National Basketball League, becoming the only all-Black team to play in a major American professional league; they disbanded when the NBL merged into the NBA.

facts.subject: Bob Douglas
facts.fact: Bob Douglas, called the Father of Black Professional Basketball, was inducted into the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame in 1972 as its first African American enshrinee.

facts.subject: Tarzan Cooper
facts.fact: Charles 'Tarzan' Cooper (August 30, 1907 - December 19, 1980), a 6-foot-4 center, played for the New York Rens from 1929 to 1941, won the 1939 world pro title with the Rens and the 1943 title with the Washington Bears, and entered the Hall of Fame in 1977.

facts.subject: Pop Gates
facts.fact: William Penn 'Pop' Gates (1917-1999) went straight from a 1938 New York City high school championship at Benjamin Franklin to a 1939 world professional championship with the Rens, leading them in scoring in the title game; he was inducted into the Hall of Fame in 1989.

facts.subject: Pop Gates
facts.fact: In October 1946 Pop Gates joined the Buffalo Bisons (soon the Tri-Cities Blackhawks), becoming with Dolly King one of two prominent African American players to integrate the National Basketball League that year.

facts.subject: Black Fives Era
facts.fact: The 'Black Fives Era' covers all-Black basketball teams from 1904 to 1950 — beginning when basketball was first introduced to African Americans on an organized scale and ending when the NBA signed its first Black players; early teams were called 'fives' after the five starters.

facts.subject: Claude Johnson
facts.fact: The terms 'Black Fives' and 'Black Fives Era' were coined and trademarked by Claude Johnson, founder of Black Fives, Inc., while researching the period.

facts.subject: Edwin Bancroft Henderson
facts.fact: Edwin Bancroft Henderson (1883-1977) learned basketball at Harvard University summer sessions and in 1904 introduced the game to African Americans on an organized scale through Washington, D.C.'s segregated public schools and the 12th Street Colored YMCA; he was inducted into the Basketball Hall of Fame in 2013.

facts.subject: Smart Set Athletic Club
facts.fact: The Smart Set Athletic Club of Brooklyn, founded in 1904, assembled the first formal fully independent African American basketball team, which debuted in 1907, and was a founding member of the Olympian Athletic League.

facts.subject: Colored Basketball World's Championship
facts.fact: The 'Colored Basketball World's Championship' was a title coined by Lester Walton of the New York Age and informally awarded by Black sportswriters to the best all-Black team each season beginning in 1907-08.

facts.subject: Cumberland Posey
facts.fact: Cumberland Posey (1890-1946) is the only person enshrined in both the National Baseball Hall of Fame (2006, for the Homestead Grays) and the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame (2016, for his Black Fives career).

facts.subject: Loendi Big Five
facts.fact: Cumberland Posey's Pittsburgh-based Loendi Big Five won four straight Colored Basketball World's Championships from 1920 to 1923; Posey had already won the title in 1912 with the Monticello Athletic Association.

facts.subject: Original Celtics
facts.fact: The Celtics were founded in 1914 as a local amateur team in Hell's Kitchen, Manhattan by Frank 'Tip' McCormack, and reconstituted in 1918 by James A. Furey and his brother Thomas as the 'Original Celtics'; the franchise was inducted into the Hall of Fame in 1959.

facts.subject: Original Celtics
facts.fact: The Original Celtics finished the 1922-23 season 193-11-1 overall, including 17-1 in league games; their dominance produced the fan cry 'Break up the Celtics!'

facts.subject: Dutch Dehnert
facts.fact: Original Celtics big man Dutch Dehnert is credited with introducing the modern concept of the pivot play.

facts.subject: Nat Holman
facts.fact: Nat Holman (1896-1995), the Original Celtics star nicknamed 'Mr. Basketball', coached CCNY to both the NCAA and NIT titles in 1950 — a sweep never achieved before or since — and was inducted into the Hall of Fame in 1964.

facts.subject: Walter Brown
facts.fact: Walter A. Brown paid James Furey a $1,000 licensing fee for the rights to use the Celtics name for his new Boston franchise in 1946.

facts.subject: Earl Lloyd
facts.fact: Earl Lloyd became the first Black player to appear in an NBA game on October 31, 1950 for the Washington Capitols, scoring 6 points; he played one day ahead of Chuck Cooper and four days before Nat Clifton purely because of how the season openers fell.

facts.subject: Earl Lloyd
facts.fact: Earl Lloyd, nicknamed 'Moon Fixer', played at West Virginia State and was drafted in the ninth round, 100th overall, of the 1950 NBA draft by the Washington Capitols; he finished with 8.4 points and 6.4 rebounds per game over 560 games.

facts.subject: Earl Lloyd
facts.fact: Earl Lloyd won the 1955 NBA championship with the Syracuse Nationals and later became the Detroit Pistons' head coach in 1971-72, going 22-55; he entered the Hall of Fame in 2003 as a contributor.

facts.subject: Chuck Cooper
facts.fact: Chuck Cooper of Duquesne became the first African American drafted by an NBA team when the Boston Celtics took him in the second round, 13th overall, of the 1950 NBA draft; he debuted November 1, 1950 and was inducted into the Hall of Fame in 2019.

facts.subject: Walter Brown
facts.fact: When drafting Chuck Cooper in 1950, Celtics owner Walter A. Brown said, 'I don't give a damn if he's striped, plaid or polka dot. Boston takes Charles Cooper of Duquesne.'

facts.subject: Nat Clifton
facts.fact: Nat 'Sweetwater' Clifton — nicknamed as a boy for his love of soft drinks — played for the New York Rens (1945-47) and the Harlem Globetrotters (1948-50) before signing with the New York Knicks on May 24, 1950 and debuting November 4, 1950.

facts.subject: Nat Clifton
facts.fact: Nat Clifton was named an NBA All-Star in 1957 at age 34, making him the oldest player in NBA history to be named a first-time All-Star.
facts.volatileNote: An 'oldest ever' record — a future older first-time All-Star would break it.

facts.subject: Harold Hunter
facts.fact: On April 26, 1950, Harold Hunter of North Carolina College became the first African American to sign a professional contract with an NBA team, the Washington Capitols; he was cut in training camp and never played an NBA game.

facts.subject: Wat Misaka
facts.fact: Wat Misaka, a 5-foot-7 Japanese American guard from Utah, was drafted 61st overall in the 1947 BAA draft by the New York Knicks and played three games in 1947-48, becoming the first non-white player in the league that became the NBA.

facts.subject: Don Barksdale
facts.fact: Don Barksdale (1923-1993) became the first African American to appear in an NBA All-Star Game in 1953, while playing for the Baltimore Bullets; he had signed with Baltimore in 1951 as a 28-year-old rookie and entered the Hall of Fame in 2012.

facts.subject: Don Barksdale
facts.fact: Don Barksdale was the first African American on the United States Olympic basketball team, winning gold with a 12-0 squad at the 1948 London Games; at UCLA he had been the first African American named a consensus All-American.

facts.subject: World Professional Basketball Tournament
facts.fact: The World Professional Basketball Tournament was an annual invitational held in Chicago from 1939 to 1948, sponsored by the Chicago Herald American; it was open to Black teams and three non-NBL teams won it — the Rens (1939), the Globetrotters (1940) and the Washington Bears (1943).

facts.subject: World Professional Basketball Tournament
facts.fact: The final World Professional Basketball Tournament, in 1948, was won by the Minneapolis Lakers, who beat the New York Rens 75-71.

facts.subject: Oregon Webfoots
facts.fact: The first NCAA men's basketball tournament was held in 1939 and was won by Oregon, which beat Ohio State 46-33 in the final. The field had eight teams.

facts.subject: NCAA tournament field size
facts.fact: The NCAA men's tournament field grew from 8 teams (1939) to 16 in 1951, 32 in 1975, 64 in 1985, 65 in 2001 (one play-in game), and 68 in 2011 with the introduction of the First Four.

facts.subject: John Wooden
facts.fact: John Wooden won 10 NCAA men's championships at UCLA in a 12-year span: 1964, 1965, 1967, 1968, 1969, 1970, 1971, 1972, 1973 and 1975.

facts.subject: UCLA Bruins
facts.fact: UCLA won seven consecutive NCAA men's championships from 1967 through 1973, a streak no other Division I program has approached.

facts.subject: UCLA Bruins
facts.fact: UCLA's NCAA-record 88-game men's winning streak ended on January 19, 1974, when Notre Dame beat the Bruins 71-70 in South Bend.

facts.subject: John Wooden
facts.fact: John Wooden was nicknamed 'the Wizard of Westwood,' a moniker he personally disliked.

facts.subject: John Wooden
facts.fact: Before coaching, John Wooden was the first three-time consensus All-American at Purdue (1930-32), and he became the first person enshrined in the Naismith Basketball Hall of Fame as both a player (1960) and a coach (1973).

facts.subject: UCLA Bruins
facts.fact: UCLA went a perfect 30-0 four times under John Wooden.

facts.subject: John Wooden
facts.fact: John Wooden's final championship came in 1975, when UCLA beat Kentucky 92-85; he retired immediately afterward at age 64.

facts.subject: Lew Alcindor / Kareem Abdul-Jabbar
facts.fact: Lew Alcindor (later Kareem Abdul-Jabbar) won three straight NCAA titles at UCLA in 1967, 1968 and 1969; the Bruins went 88-2 in his three varsity seasons.

facts.subject: the dunk ban
facts.fact: The NCAA banned dunking after Lew Alcindor's sophomore season; the restriction, widely called 'the Alcindor Rule,' stayed in effect until the 1976-77 season.

facts.subject: Lew Alcindor / Kareem Abdul-Jabbar
facts.fact: Lew Alcindor won the NCAA tournament Most Outstanding Player award three straight years, 1967 through 1969.
facts.volatileNote: A future player could match or break the three-MOP mark.

facts.subject: Lew Alcindor / Kareem Abdul-Jabbar
facts.fact: In 1965 Alcindor's UCLA freshman team beat the defending national champion UCLA varsity 75-60 in an exhibition; the freshman squad went 21-0 with Alcindor averaging 33 points and 21 rebounds.

facts.subject: Texas Western Miners
facts.fact: Texas Western beat Kentucky 72-65 for the 1966 NCAA title at Cole Field House, with Don Haskins starting five Black players against Adolph Rupp's all-white starting five. The school is now UTEP.

facts.subject: Jerry Chambers
facts.fact: The 1966 Final Four Most Outstanding Player was Jerry Chambers of Utah, whose team lost in the national semifinal and never reached the title game.

facts.subject: Loyola Chicago Ramblers
facts.fact: Loyola Chicago beat Cincinnati 60-58 in overtime for the 1963 NCAA title, denying the Bearcats a third straight championship. George Ireland coached the Ramblers, who started four Black players.

facts.subject: the Game of Change
facts.fact: Loyola Chicago's 1963 Mideast regional win over all-white Mississippi State, whose team defied a state ban on playing integrated opponents, is known as the 'Game of Change.'

facts.subject: Art Heyman
facts.fact: The 1963 Final Four Most Outstanding Player was Art Heyman of Duke, whose team finished third.

facts.subject: 1957 NCAA final
facts.fact: North Carolina beat Kansas 54-53 in triple overtime for the 1957 title on March 23, 1957, one night after also winning a triple-overtime semifinal against Michigan State. Frank McGuire coached the Tar Heels.

facts.subject: Wilt Chamberlain
facts.fact: Wilt Chamberlain of Kansas was named 1957 Final Four Most Outstanding Player despite losing the championship game.

facts.subject: UCLA vs Houston 1968
facts.fact: On January 20, 1968, Houston beat UCLA 71-69 in the 'Game of the Century' at the Astrodome before 52,693 fans; it was the first NCAA regular-season game broadcast nationwide in prime time.

facts.subject: UCLA vs Houston 1968 rematch
facts.fact: UCLA avenged the Game of the Century by crushing Houston 101-69 in the 1968 Final Four semifinal, a 32-point margin, then won the national title.

facts.subject: Bill Walton
facts.fact: Bill Walton scored 44 points on 21-of-22 shooting with 13 rebounds in UCLA's 87-66 win over Memphis State in the 1973 title game — still the NCAA championship-game scoring record.
facts.volatileNote: A future title-game performance could surpass 44 points.

facts.subject: Indiana Hoosiers
facts.fact: Indiana's 1976 team is the most recent men's national champion to finish a season undefeated.
facts.volatileNote: Would change if another team ever goes undefeated and wins the title.

facts.subject: 1979 NCAA final
facts.fact: Michigan State beat Indiana State 75-64 on March 26, 1979 in Salt Lake City; Magic Johnson was Most Outstanding Player, Larry Bird's Sycamores entered undefeated, and it remains the highest-rated televised college basketball game ever.

facts.subject: 1982 NCAA final
facts.fact: North Carolina beat Georgetown 63-62 for the 1982 title at the Louisiana Superdome; freshman Michael Jordan hit the go-ahead jumper with 17 seconds left, then Georgetown's Fred Brown mistakenly passed to James Worthy. Dean Smith won his first title.

facts.subject: James Worthy
facts.fact: James Worthy was the 1982 Final Four Most Outstanding Player after a game-high 28 points in the championship win over Georgetown; Michael Jordan scored 16 and Patrick Ewing had 23 and 10.

facts.subject: 1983 NCAA final
facts.fact: Sixth-seeded NC State beat Houston 54-52 in the 1983 title game when Lorenzo Charles caught Dereck Whittenburg's roughly 30-foot airball and dunked it at the buzzer. Jim Valvano coached the Wolfpack; Houston was nicknamed Phi Slama Jama.

facts.subject: Akeem Olajuwon
facts.fact: Houston's Akeem Olajuwon was the 1983 Final Four Most Outstanding Player and remains the last player to win the award while playing for a team that failed to win the national title.
facts.volatileNote: Ends if a future MOP again comes from a non-championship team.

facts.subject: Villanova Wildcats
facts.fact: Eighth-seeded Villanova beat Georgetown 66-64 for the 1985 title — still the lowest seed ever to win the men's championship. Rollie Massimino coached; Ed Pinckney was Most Outstanding Player.
facts.volatileNote: Would change if a lower seed ever won the title.

facts.subject: 1985 NCAA final
facts.fact: The 1985 Villanova-Georgetown final was the last NCAA championship game played without a shot clock, and 1985 was the first year of the 64-team bracket.

facts.subject: 1988 Kansas Jayhawks
facts.fact: The 1988 Kansas 'Danny and the Miracles' team finished 27-11 and beat Oklahoma 83-79 for the title — the most losses ever by an NCAA champion. Larry Brown coached; Danny Manning was Most Outstanding Player.

facts.subject: Christian Laettner
facts.fact: On March 28, 1992, Christian Laettner hit a turnaround buzzer-beater to beat Kentucky in overtime in the East Regional final, finishing a perfect 10-of-10 from the field and 10-of-10 from the line for 31 points. Duke trailed by one with 2.1 seconds left.

facts.subject: Christian Laettner
facts.fact: Christian Laettner holds the NCAA tournament career scoring record with 407 points, playing 23 of a possible 24 tournament games and winning 21.
facts.volatileNote: Career tournament scoring record could be broken.

facts.subject: Duke Blue Devils
facts.fact: Duke won back-to-back titles in 1991 and 1992, the first repeat champion since UCLA in 1973.

facts.subject: Chris Webber
facts.fact: In the 1993 title game, with Michigan trailing North Carolina 73-71 and about 11 seconds left, Chris Webber called a timeout his team did not have; the technical foul sealed a 77-71 North Carolina win.

facts.subject: Michigan Fab Five
facts.fact: Michigan's Fab Five, recruited in the 1991 class, were Chris Webber, Jalen Rose, Juwan Howard, Jimmy King and Ray Jackson. They lost the 1992 final to Duke 71-51 and the 1993 final to North Carolina 77-71; Michigan later vacated both Final Four runs.

facts.subject: Bryce Drew
facts.fact: In 1998, No. 13 Valparaiso beat No. 4 Ole Miss 70-69 on a play called 'Pacer': Jamie Sykes inbounded to Bill Jenkins, who touch-passed to Bryce Drew for a 23-foot three with 2.5 seconds left. Bryce's father Homer Drew was the head coach.

facts.subject: Carmelo Anthony
facts.fact: Freshman Carmelo Anthony led Syracuse past Kansas 81-78 for the 2003 title with 20 points and 10 rebounds, winning Most Outstanding Player. It was the first national championship for Syracuse and for coach Jim Boeheim; Hakim Warrick blocked Michael Lee's three with 1.5 seconds left.

facts.subject: Carmelo Anthony
facts.fact: Carmelo Anthony scored 33 points against Texas in the 2003 national semifinal, an NCAA tournament record for a freshman.

facts.subject: Kevin Durant
facts.fact: Kevin Durant averaged 25.8 points and 11.1 rebounds in his lone season at Texas (2006-07) and became the first freshman to win a national player of the year award, taking both the Naismith and Wooden. Texas lost in the second round to USC; he was drafted second in 2007.

facts.subject: Anthony Davis
facts.fact: Anthony Davis was named 2012 Final Four Most Outstanding Player after posting just 6 points with 16 rebounds and 6 blocks in Kentucky's title-game win over Kansas. He set a freshman record with 186 blocks that season and went first overall in the 2012 draft.

facts.subject: 2015 Kentucky Wildcats
facts.fact: John Calipari's Kentucky team reached the 2015 Final Four at 38-0 before losing 71-64 to Wisconsin in the national semifinal.

facts.subject: Duke Blue Devils
facts.fact: Duke beat Wisconsin 68-63 at Lucas Oil Stadium for the 2015 title, Mike Krzyzewski's fifth championship; Tyus Jones was Most Outstanding Player.

facts.subject: Mike Krzyzewski
facts.fact: Mike Krzyzewski retired with a 1,202-368 Division I record, the most men's Division I wins ever, plus five national titles (1991, 1992, 2001, 2010, 2015), a record 13 Final Fours, and 42 seasons at Duke.

facts.subject: Kris Jenkins
facts.fact: Kris Jenkins hit a three at the buzzer to give Villanova a 77-74 win over North Carolina in the 2016 title game, moments after Marcus Paige's double-clutch three had tied it. Ryan Arcidiacono was Most Outstanding Player and it was Jay Wright's first title.

facts.subject: Middle Tennessee Blue Raiders
facts.fact: No. 15 Middle Tennessee beat No. 2 Michigan State 90-81 in the 2016 first round, the eighth 15-over-2 upset in tournament history.

facts.subject: UMBC Retrievers
facts.fact: UMBC became the first No. 16 seed to beat a No. 1 seed in the men's NCAA tournament, routing Virginia 74-54 in 2018.

facts.subject: Loyola Chicago Ramblers
facts.fact: Loyola Chicago, an 11 seed backed by 98-year-old chaplain Sister Jean, reached the 2018 Final Four — the fourth 11 seed to do so.

facts.subject: Donte DiVincenzo
facts.fact: Villanova beat Michigan 79-62 for the 2018 title, and reserve Donte DiVincenzo scored 31 points off the bench and was named Most Outstanding Player.

facts.subject: Saint Peter's Peacocks
facts.fact: No. 15 Saint Peter's beat Kentucky 85-79 in overtime, Murray State 70-60 and Purdue 67-64 in 2022 to become the first 15 seed to reach the Elite Eight. Shaheen Holloway was the coach.

facts.subject: 2022 Kansas Jayhawks
facts.fact: Kansas beat North Carolina 72-69 for the 2022 title after erasing a 16-point first-half deficit, the largest comeback in championship game history. Ochai Agbaji was Most Outstanding Player.

facts.subject: Fairleigh Dickinson Knights
facts.fact: No. 16 Fairleigh Dickinson beat No. 1 Purdue 63-58 in 2023, only the second 16-over-1 upset in men's tournament history.

facts.subject: UConn Huskies
facts.fact: UConn beat San Diego State 76-59 at NRG Stadium in Houston for the 2023 title, the program's fifth and Dan Hurley's first. Adama Sanogo was Most Outstanding Player with 118 tournament points.

facts.subject: Florida Atlantic Owls
facts.fact: Ninth-seeded Florida Atlantic reached its first Final Four in 2023 by beating No. 3 Kansas State 79-76, only the second 9 seed since 1985 to make the Final Four.

facts.subject: Princeton Tigers
facts.fact: No. 15 Princeton beat No. 2 Arizona 59-55 in 2023 and then beat Missouri to reach the Sweet 16.

facts.subject: UConn Huskies
facts.fact: UConn beat Purdue 75-60 in the 2024 final to win back-to-back national championships, its sixth title overall.

facts.subject: Florida Gators
facts.fact: Florida beat Houston 65-63 in the 2025 national championship game under coach Todd Golden.

facts.subject: Michigan Wolverines
facts.fact: Michigan beat UConn 69-63 in the 2026 national championship game at Lucas Oil Stadium in Indianapolis for its second title. Dusty May won his first championship and Elliot Cadeau was Most Outstanding Player.

facts.subject: High Point Panthers
facts.fact: No. 12 High Point beat No. 5 Wisconsin in the 2026 first round, the biggest first-round upset of that tournament and High Point's first-ever NCAA tournament win.

facts.subject: Pete Maravich
facts.fact: Pete Maravich scored 3,667 points in 83 varsity games at LSU from 1967-70, averaging 44.2 per game — still the NCAA Division I men's career scoring record, compiled entirely before the three-point line existed.
facts.volatileNote: Men's Division I career scoring record could theoretically be broken.

facts.subject: Pete Maravich
facts.fact: Maravich's 1969-70 season — 1,381 points in 31 games, 44.5 per game — is the NCAA Division I single-season scoring average record. He led the nation in scoring all three varsity seasons.
facts.volatileNote: Single-season scoring average record could be broken.

facts.subject: Frank Selvy
facts.fact: Frank Selvy of Furman scored 100 points against Newberry on February 13, 1954 — the only 100-point game by a Division I player. He shot 41-of-66 from the field and 18-of-22 from the line and averaged 41.7 points that season.
facts.volatileNote: Another Division I player could theoretically score 100.

facts.subject: Louisiana Tech Lady Techsters
facts.fact: Louisiana Tech beat Cheyney State 76-62 in the first NCAA Division I women's championship game in 1982 at Norfolk Scope. Sonja Hogg coached; Janice Lawrence was Most Outstanding Player. The 32-team field replaced the AIAW tournament.

facts.subject: Pat Summitt
facts.fact: Pat Summitt went 1,098-208 in 38 seasons at Tennessee (1974-2012), never had a losing season and never missed the NCAA tournament. She was hired at age 22 and became the winningest coach in NCAA basketball history in 2005.

facts.subject: Pat Summitt
facts.fact: Pat Summitt won eight NCAA women's championships at Tennessee: 1987, 1989, 1991, 1996, 1997, 1998, 2007 and 2008.

facts.subject: UConn Huskies women
facts.fact: UConn's women won 111 straight games from November 23, 2014 until March 31, 2017, when Mississippi State's Morgan William hit an overtime buzzer-beater for a 66-64 Final Four win.
facts.volatileNote: Longest winning streak record could be broken.

facts.subject: Geno Auriemma
facts.fact: Geno Auriemma has won 12 NCAA women's championships at UConn (1995, 2000, 2002, 2003, 2004, 2009, 2010, 2013, 2014, 2015, 2016, 2025), more than any coach in college basketball history.
facts.volatileNote: Auriemma is still coaching and can add titles.

facts.subject: UConn Huskies women
facts.volatileNote: UConn could add another perfect season.

facts.subject: Breanna Stewart
facts.fact: Breanna Stewart won four consecutive NCAA championships at UConn from 2013 to 2016 and was named Final Four Most Outstanding Player all four years.

facts.subject: Sheryl Swoopes
facts.fact: Sheryl Swoopes scored 47 points on 16 field goals for Texas Tech against Ohio State in the 1993 NCAA women's championship game, a title-game record.
facts.volatileNote: Title-game scoring record could be broken.

facts.subject: Caitlin Clark
facts.fact: Caitlin Clark finished her Iowa career with 3,951 points, the most in NCAA Division I history for men or women. She passed Pete Maravich's 3,667 on March 3, 2024 against Ohio State and made a Division I record 548 three-pointers.
facts.volatileNote: All-time NCAA Division I scoring record could be broken.

facts.subject: Caitlin Clark
facts.fact: In the 2023 NCAA tournament Caitlin Clark set records with 191 points and 60 assists, hit 8 threes in the championship game, and became the first player in tournament history with back-to-back 40-point games.
facts.volatileNote: Single-tournament records could be broken.

facts.subject: Kim Mulkey
facts.fact: LSU beat Iowa 102-85 for the 2023 NCAA women's title, Kim Mulkey's fourth championship as a head coach after three at Baylor (2005, 2012, 2019). Angel Reese was Most Outstanding Player.

facts.subject: Brittney Griner
facts.fact: Brittney Griner blocked 748 shots in four seasons at Baylor, the NCAA women's career record, and dunked 18 times in college. She had 26 points, 13 rebounds and 5 blocks in Baylor's 80-61 title-game win over Notre Dame in 2012 and went first overall in the 2013 WNBA draft.
facts.volatileNote: Career blocks record could be broken.

facts.subject: 2012 Baylor Lady Bears
facts.fact: Baylor went 40-0 in 2011-12, the first team in NCAA basketball history — men's or women's — to win 40 games in a season.

facts.subject: UConn Huskies women
facts.fact: UConn beat South Carolina 82-59 in the 2025 NCAA women's championship game for its 12th national title.

facts.subject: UCLA Bruins women
facts.fact: UCLA beat South Carolina 79-51 in the 2026 NCAA women's championship game in Phoenix for its first women's national title in the NCAA era. Cori Close won her first championship and Lauren Betts was Most Outstanding Player.

facts.subject: Nancy Lieberman
facts.fact: Nancy Lieberman won back-to-back AIAW national championships at Old Dominion in 1979 and 1980, plus a WNIT title in 1978.

facts.subject: BIG3 league
facts.fact: The BIG3 was founded on January 11, 2017 by rapper and actor Ice Cube along with entertainment executive Jeff Kwatinetz, and played its first season that summer.

facts.subject: BIG3 format
facts.fact: The BIG3 is played 3-on-3 on a half court, with five players on each roster.

facts.subject: BIG3 scoring
facts.fact: A BIG3 game is won by the first team to reach 50 or more points with a lead of at least two; there is no overtime period.

facts.subject: BIG3 4-point circles
facts.fact: BIG3 courts have three 4-point circles located 30 feet from the basket — one at the midline and two at 40-degree angles.

facts.subject: BIG3 shot clock
facts.fact: The BIG3 uses a 14-second shot clock.

facts.subject: BIG3 halftime
facts.fact: BIG3 halftime is triggered when either team reaches 25 points rather than by a game clock.

facts.subject: BIG3 clearing rule
facts.fact: In the BIG3 the ball must be cleared after a change of possession — the ball handler establishes both feet behind the three-point line before the team can score.

facts.subject: BIG3 fouls
facts.fact: After a team's fifth foul in a BIG3 half, the opponent receives two one-point free throws plus possession.

facts.subject: Trilogy
facts.fact: Trilogy won the inaugural 2017 BIG3 championship, beating 3 Headed Monsters 51-46 at MGM Grand Garden Arena in Las Vegas on August 26, 2017, to finish a perfect 10-0.

facts.subject: Rashard Lewis
facts.fact: Rashard Lewis of the 3 Headed Monsters was the BIG3's first league MVP, in 2017.

facts.subject: BIG3 debut
facts.fact: The BIG3's first games were played June 25, 2017 at Barclays Center in Brooklyn, New York; the 2017 regular season drew 99,187 fans across 32 games.

facts.subject: Rick Mahorn
facts.fact: Rick Mahorn coached Trilogy, captained by Kenyon Martin, to the 2017 BIG3 title and was the league's first Coach of the Year.

facts.subject: James White
facts.fact: James White of Trilogy was the BIG3's first Defensive Player of the Year, in 2017.

facts.subject: Power
facts.fact: Power beat 3's Company 51-43 at Barclays Center on August 24, 2018 for the BIG3 title; Corey Maggette was league MVP and Player Captain of the Year after Power went 7-1 in the regular season.

facts.subject: Nancy Lieberman
facts.fact: Nancy Lieberman coached Power to the 2018 BIG3 title and was Coach of the Year, becoming the first woman to coach a men's professional basketball team to a championship. She had already been the first woman to head-coach a men's pro team, with the NBA D-League's Texas Legends in 2009.

facts.subject: Chris Andersen
facts.fact: Chris 'Birdman' Andersen of Power was the 2018 BIG3 Defensive Player of the Year.

facts.subject: Triplets
facts.fact: The Triplets beat the Killer 3's 50-39 at Staples Center in Los Angeles on September 1, 2019 for the BIG3 title. Joe Johnson was league MVP at 21.9 points per game and also led the league in assists.

facts.subject: Lisa Leslie
facts.fact: Lisa Leslie coached the Triplets to the 2019 BIG3 championship and was named Coach of the Year.

facts.subject: Amar'e Stoudemire
facts.fact: Amar'e Stoudemire of Tri-State was the 2019 BIG3 Defensive Player of the Year, leading the league at 1.8 blocks per game. Reggie Evans led in rebounding at 10.9 per game.

facts.subject: BIG3 league
facts.fact: The BIG3 cancelled its 2020 season because of the COVID-19 pandemic, returning in 2021.

facts.subject: Trilogy
facts.fact: Trilogy has won the most BIG3 championships with three: 2017, 2021 and 2022.
facts.volatileNote: Another franchise could tie or pass three titles.

facts.subject: Enemies
facts.fact: The Enemies beat the Triplets for the 2023 BIG3 championship, with the title game played in London.

facts.subject: Bivouac
facts.fact: Bivouac won its first BIG3 championship in 2024, beating 3's Company in the title game in Boston.

facts.subject: Miami 305
facts.fact: For 2025 the BIG3 abandoned its barnstorming tour model for city-based franchises; Miami 305 beat the Chicago Triplets for the championship, played in Orlando.

facts.subject: Clyde Drexler
facts.fact: Hall of Famer Clyde Drexler became BIG3 commissioner in 2018, succeeding Roger Mason Jr., who held the role from 2017 to 2018.

facts.subject: BIG3 head coaches
facts.fact: BIG3 head coaches have included Julius Erving, Gary Payton, Charles Oakley, Rick Barry, George Gervin, Rick Mahorn, Nancy Lieberman, Michael Cooper, Lisa Leslie and Stephen Jackson.

facts.subject: Allen Iverson
facts.fact: Allen Iverson joined the BIG3 as player-coach of 3's Company.

facts.subject: Jaylen Brown
facts.fact: Jaylen Brown played in the 2023 BIG3 All-Star Game, a rare appearance by an active NBA player in the league.

facts.subject: James Naismith
facts.fact: James Naismith invented basketball in December 1891 at the International YMCA Training School (now Springfield College) in Springfield, Massachusetts, as an indoor game to occupy a rowdy class during a harsh New England winter.

facts.subject: James Naismith
facts.fact: Naismith was Canadian, born November 6, 1861, in Almonte, Canada West (now Ontario); he later became a naturalized American.

facts.subject: the first baskets
facts.fact: The first goals were peach baskets nailed to the gymnasium balcony roughly 10 feet above the floor — the same rim height used at every level today.

facts.subject: the first basketball
facts.fact: The first games were played with a soccer ball; in 1894 Naismith had Spalding produce the first purpose-built basketball.

facts.subject: the first basketball game
facts.fact: The first basketball game was played December 21, 1891, and ended 1–0.

facts.subject: William R. Chase
facts.fact: The only basket in the first basketball game was scored by Chase (William R. Chase), one of Naismith's 18 students.

facts.subject: the first basketball game
facts.fact: Naismith divided his class of eighteen students into two teams of nine players each for the first game.

facts.subject: Naismith's original rules
facts.fact: Naismith wrote exactly 13 original rules for the game; they were published January 15, 1892.

facts.subject: Naismith's Rule 3
facts.fact: Original Rule 3: "A player cannot run with the ball; the player must throw it from the spot on which he catches it" — dribbling did not exist in Naismith's rules.

facts.subject: Naismith's Rule 2
facts.fact: Original Rule 2 allowed the ball to be batted in any direction with one or both hands, but never with the fist.

facts.subject: Naismith's Rule 7
facts.fact: Original Rule 7: three consecutive fouls by one side counted as a goal for the opponents — there were no free throws in the original game.

facts.subject: Naismith's Rule 12
facts.fact: Original Rule 12 set the game at two fifteen-minute halves with five minutes of rest between them.

facts.subject: Naismith's Rule 9
facts.fact: Original Rule 9 gave the player throwing the ball in from out of bounds five seconds to release it — the five-second inbound limit is one of the few original rules still in force.

facts.subject: Naismith's Rules 10 and 11
facts.fact: Under the original rules the umpire was judge of the players and noted fouls, while the referee was judge of the ball and kept the time.

facts.subject: Naismith's Rule 13
facts.fact: Original Rule 13: the side making the most goals wins; in the event of a draw the captains could agree to continue play until another goal was made.

facts.subject: Naismith's original rules document
facts.fact: In December 2010 Naismith's two-page typed original rules sold at auction for $4,338,500 to David and Suzanne Booth, who donated the document to the University of Kansas.

facts.subject: James Naismith
facts.fact: Naismith coached basketball at the University of Kansas, finishing 55–60 — the only coach in Kansas history with a losing record.

facts.subject: hoops and backboards
facts.fact: Metal hoops, nets and backboards were introduced by 1906; before the basket bottoms were opened, someone had to fetch the ball after every made shot.

facts.subject: professional basketball
facts.fact: The first professional basketball league was founded in 1898.

facts.subject: the BAA and NBA
facts.fact: The Basketball Association of America was founded June 6, 1946, and became the National Basketball Association in 1949 after absorbing the National Basketball League.

facts.subject: Senda Berenson
facts.fact: Senda Berenson, an instructor at Smith College, organized the earliest women's games in the 1890s using adjusted rules.

facts.subject: Danny Biasone
facts.fact: Danny Biasone, owner of the Syracuse Nationals — working with general manager Leo Ferris — created the 24-second shot clock, adopted by the NBA for the 1954–55 season.

facts.subject: the 24-second math
facts.fact: Biasone got 24 seconds by taking the 2,880 seconds in a 48-minute game and dividing by 120 — his estimate of the total shots (about 60 per team) in a well-played game.

facts.subject: the 19-18 game
facts.fact: The November 22, 1950 game in which Fort Wayne beat Minneapolis 19–18 — the lowest-scoring game in NBA history — is the stall-fest most often cited as proof the league needed a shot clock.

facts.subject: NCAA men's shot clock
facts.fact: NCAA men's basketball adopted a 45-second shot clock in 1985–86, cut it to 35 seconds in 1993–94, and cut it again to 30 seconds in 2015–16.
facts.volatileNote: The current NCAA men's shot clock length could be shortened again by rules committee action.

facts.subject: FIBA shot clock
facts.fact: FIBA used a 30-second shot clock from 1956 and shortened it to 24 seconds in 2000.

facts.subject: WNBA shot clock
facts.fact: The WNBA began with a 30-second shot clock and shortened it to 24 seconds in 2006.

facts.subject: the 14-second reset
facts.fact: Since 2018 the NBA resets the shot clock to 14 seconds (not 24) when the offense rebounds its own miss that hit the rim.

facts.subject: shot clock violation
facts.fact: When a team fails to get a shot off in time, the ball is awarded to the defensive team on the sideline nearest where play stopped, no closer to the baseline than the free throw line extended.

facts.subject: NBA court dimensions
facts.fact: An NBA court measures 94 feet long by 50 feet wide.

facts.subject: FIBA court dimensions
facts.fact: A FIBA international court measures 28 by 15 meters (about 91.9 by 49.2 feet), slightly smaller than an NBA court.

facts.subject: rim height
facts.fact: The upper edge of the ring is 10 feet above and parallel to the floor at every major level of the game.

facts.subject: rim diameter
facts.fact: The basket ring is 18 inches in inside diameter and is painted orange.

facts.subject: rim placement
facts.fact: The nearest point of the ring sits 6 inches from the plane of the face of the backboard.

facts.subject: backboard dimensions
facts.fact: A regulation backboard is a rectangle 6 feet horizontally by 3½ feet vertically (72 by 42 inches).

facts.subject: backboard inner square
facts.fact: The white target rectangle on the backboard measures 24 inches horizontally by 18 inches vertically, with a 2-inch border.

facts.subject: free throw line
facts.fact: The free throw line is 15 feet from the plane of the face of the backboard.

facts.subject: NBA lane width
facts.fact: The NBA free throw lane is 16 feet wide; FIBA's rectangular lane is 4.9 m (about 16 feet).

facts.subject: the lane widening of 1951
facts.fact: The NBA doubled the lane from 6 feet to 12 feet at the start of the 1951–52 season, a change driven by George Mikan's dominance in the paint.

facts.subject: the lane widening of 1964
facts.fact: The NBA widened the lane again from 12 feet to 16 feet for the 1964–65 season, chiefly to reduce Wilt Chamberlain's effectiveness near the basket.

facts.subject: "the key"
facts.fact: The painted area is called "the key" because the original 6-foot-wide lane topped by the free-throw circle looked like a keyhole.

facts.subject: NCAA lane width
facts.fact: The NCAA and NAIA free throw lane is 12 feet wide — four feet narrower than the NBA's.
facts.volatileNote: NCAA has periodically discussed widening its lane toward the NBA/FIBA standard.

facts.subject: the FIBA lane
facts.fact: FIBA replaced its trapezoidal lane — 3.6 m at the free throw line flaring to 6 m at the endline — with a rectangle in 2010.

facts.subject: restricted area
facts.fact: The restricted-area arc, inside which a secondary defender cannot draw a charge, extends 4 feet from the center of the basket ring in the NBA and NCAA (1.25 m in FIBA).

facts.subject: center circle
facts.fact: The NBA center circle has a 6-foot radius — 12 feet in diameter; FIBA's is 3.6 m across.

facts.subject: men's basketball size
facts.fact: A men's regulation (size 7) basketball has a circumference of 29.5 inches (75 cm) and weighs 20–22 ounces.

facts.subject: women's basketball size
facts.fact: The women's ball (size 6), used by the WNBA, NCAA women and FIBA women, has a circumference of 28.5 inches (72 cm) and weighs 18–19 ounces.

facts.subject: ball inflation
facts.fact: NBA officials must check that the game ball is inflated to between 7½ and 8½ pounds of pressure before tip-off.

facts.subject: NBA game ball supplier
facts.fact: Wilson supplied the NBA's game ball from 1946 to 1983, Spalding from 1983 to 2021, and Wilson took the contract back beginning with the 2021–22 season.
facts.volatileNote: The NBA's ball supplier is a contract that can change again.

facts.subject: the ABA ball
facts.fact: From 1967 through 1976 the American Basketball Association used a distinctive red, white and blue basketball.

facts.subject: the 2006 microfiber ball
facts.fact: The NBA switched to a synthetic microfiber composite ball in 2006; players hated it and the league returned to the traditional leather ball partway through that season.

facts.subject: the first three-point line
facts.fact: The American Basketball League, run by Harlem Globetrotters owner Abe Saperstein, became the first league to use a three-point line, in 1961.

facts.subject: the ABA three-pointer
facts.fact: The ABA used the three-point shot from its first season, 1967–68, as a marketing hook against the NBA.

facts.subject: the NBA's first three-pointer
facts.fact: The NBA adopted the three-point line for 1979–80; Chris Ford of the Boston Celtics made the league's first three-pointer on October 12, 1979.

facts.subject: the shortened three-point line
facts.fact: From 1994–95 through 1996–97 the NBA shortened the three-point line to a uniform 22 feet all the way around, then restored 23 feet 9 inches for 1997–98.

facts.subject: NBA three-point distance
facts.fact: The NBA three-point arc is 23 feet 9 inches from the middle of the basket, but the line runs straight 3 feet inside the sidelines, making the corner three only 22 feet.

facts.subject: NCAA three-point line
facts.fact: The NCAA adopted the three-pointer nationally at 19 feet 9 inches beginning in 1986–87, and it debuted in the NCAA tournament in March 1987.

facts.subject: FIBA three-point line
facts.fact: FIBA introduced the three-point line in 1984 at 6.25 meters and used it at the Olympics for the first time in 1988; the arc is now 6.75 meters.

facts.subject: traveling
facts.fact: In the NBA and FIBA a player who receives the ball while moving may take two steps in coming to a stop, passing or shooting; the pivot foot may be lifted but not returned to the floor before the ball is released.

facts.subject: three-second rule
facts.fact: The offensive three-second lane violation was introduced in 1936, largely in response to the rough 1935 Kentucky–NYU game at Madison Square Garden in which Leroy Edwards was mauled in the post.

facts.subject: defensive three seconds
facts.fact: The NBA added the defensive three-second rule for 2001–02: a defender who spends more than three seconds in the lane without actively guarding anyone gives up a team technical foul — one free throw, and the offense keeps the ball. The WNBA adopted it in 2013; FIBA has no such rule.

facts.subject: backcourt eight-second rule
facts.fact: An NBA team may not be in continuous possession in its backcourt for more than 8 consecutive seconds; NCAA men still use 10 seconds.

facts.subject: five-second inbound rule
facts.fact: A player throwing the ball in must release it within 5 seconds or the ball goes to the other team.

facts.subject: back-to-the-basket five seconds
facts.fact: NBA rules forbid an offensive player below the free throw line extended from dribbling with his back or side to the basket for more than five seconds.

facts.subject: goaltending
facts.fact: The NCAA outlawed defensive goaltending in 1944; before 6-foot-10 centers like George Mikan arrived, swatting a descending ball off the rim was thought physically impossible.

facts.subject: goaltending
facts.fact: Goaltending is touching a shot on its downward flight toward the basket, while it is on the rim, or while it is inside the imaginary cylinder above the rim.

facts.subject: backcourt violation
facts.fact: A backcourt (over-and-back) violation occurs when a player is the first to touch a ball that he or a teammate caused to go from frontcourt to backcourt while his team was in control.

facts.subject: fouling out
facts.fact: A player fouls out of an NBA game on his sixth personal foul; under NCAA and FIBA rules (40-minute games) it is the fifth.

facts.subject: the penalty/bonus
facts.fact: Each NBA team is allowed four team fouls per regulation period without extra penalty, so the fifth team foul of a quarter puts the opponent in the bonus; in overtime the limit is three.

facts.subject: flagrant fouls
facts.fact: A flagrant foul type 1 is contact judged unnecessary; a type 2 is contact judged unnecessary AND excessive and brings immediate ejection. Both award two free throws and the ball at the free throw line extended.

facts.subject: technical fouls
facts.fact: A technical foul in the NBA awards the other team one free throw, and two unsportsmanlike technicals in a game bring automatic ejection.

facts.subject: clear path foul
facts.fact: A clear-path-to-the-basket foul costs the defense two free throws plus possession of the ball on the sideline nearest where play was interrupted.

facts.subject: free throws
facts.fact: A made free throw is worth one point, and the shooter must release the attempt within ten seconds.

facts.subject: the one-and-one
facts.fact: In traditional NCAA rules the one-and-one bonus starts on the seventh team foul of a half (make the first to earn a second) and the double bonus — two shots regardless — starts on the tenth.
facts.volatileNote: NCAA bonus formats have been revised (women moved to per-quarter fouls in 2015-16) and could change again.

facts.subject: Rick Barry
facts.fact: Rick Barry shot his free throws underhanded — the "granny" style — and retired as the NBA's career free-throw percentage leader at about 90%.

facts.subject: NBA game length
facts.fact: All regulation periods in the NBA are twelve minutes, for a 48-minute game; overtime periods are five minutes.

facts.subject: 40-minute games
facts.fact: FIBA, the WNBA and NCAA women's basketball all play four 10-minute quarters (40 minutes), while NCAA men play two 20-minute halves.

facts.subject: NBA timeouts
facts.fact: Each NBA team gets seven charged timeouts in regulation, no more than four of which may be used in the fourth period, plus two per overtime.
facts.volatileNote: The NBA restructured timeout counts in 2017 and could revise them again.

facts.subject: NBA officiating crew
facts.fact: Three officials work the floor in an NBA game — a crew chief, a referee and an umpire — supported by a Replay Center Official, an official scorer, two timers and a courtside administrator.

facts.subject: officiating positions
facts.fact: In three-person officiating mechanics the lead works the baseline, the trail is level with the three-point line, and the center stands near the free throw line extended on the opposite side.

facts.subject: alternating possession arrow
facts.fact: Men's college basketball replaced most jump balls with the alternating-possession arrow in 1981–82; women's college followed in 1986–87 and FIBA adopted the arrow in 2003. The NBA and WNBA still hold real jump balls.

facts.subject: the center jump
facts.fact: Basketball originally restarted with a jump ball after every made basket; college eliminated the center jump in 1937 and the NBA followed in 1949.

facts.subject: the Elam Ending
facts.fact: The Elam Ending, invented by Ball State professor Nick Elam, shuts off the game clock late and plays to a target score; The Basketball Tournament adopted it in 2017 and the 2020 NBA All-Star Game set its target at the leader's score after three quarters plus 24 points, honoring Kobe Bryant.

facts.subject: zone defense in the NBA
facts.fact: The NBA scrapped its illegal-defense rules and legalized zone defense beginning with the 2001–02 season, pairing the change with the new defensive three-second violation.

facts.subject: box-and-one
facts.fact: A box-and-one is a combination defense in which four defenders play a box zone and the fifth guards one opponent man-to-man; a triangle-and-two puts three in a zone and two in man coverage.

facts.subject: the dunk ban
facts.fact: Dunking was banned in college basketball from 1967 to 1976 under what became known as the "Lew Alcindor rule," named for the UCLA center later known as Kareem Abdul-Jabbar.

facts.subject: "slam dunk"
facts.fact: Longtime Lakers broadcaster Chick Hearn is credited with coining the phrase "slam dunk."

facts.subject: position numbers
facts.fact: The five positions are numbered 1 through 5: point guard, shooting guard, small forward, power forward and center — the center also called the pivot or the five.

facts.subject: position nicknames
facts.fact: A "stretch four" is a power forward who shoots from three-point range; a "swingman" plays both shooting guard and small forward; a "point forward" is a forward who runs the offense.

facts.subject: shooting slang
facts.fact: A swish goes through the net without touching the rim; an airball hits neither rim nor backboard; a brick clangs hard off the rim.

facts.subject: "charity stripe"
facts.fact: "Charity stripe" is slang for the free throw line, because the points there come uncontested.

facts.subject: "cherry picking"
facts.fact: Cherry picking is when a player skips playing defense and lingers near his own offensive basket waiting for an easy outlet pass and layup.

facts.subject: triple-double
facts.fact: A triple-double is double-digit figures in three positive statistical categories in a single game; a quadruple-double is four.

facts.subject: backdoor cut
facts.fact: A backdoor cut is when a perimeter player steps away from the basket to pull his defender out, then suddenly cuts behind him to the rim for a pass.

facts.subject: Euro step
facts.fact: The Euro step is a move in which a player picks up his dribble, steps hard in one direction, then takes a second step in another direction to get around a defender.

facts.subject: pick and roll
facts.fact: In a pick and roll, one player sets a screen for the ball handler and then slips behind the defender toward the basket to receive a pass.

facts.subject: traveling signal
facts.fact: Officials signal traveling by rotating their fists one over the other in front of the chest.

facts.subject: three-point signals
facts.fact: An official raises one arm with three fingers extended to signal a three-point attempt, and extends both arms straight overhead to signal a successful three.

facts.subject: blocking signal
facts.fact: An official signals a blocking foul by placing both hands on the hips; a player-control (charging) foul is signaled with a fist punched forward while the other hand is placed behind the head.

facts.subject: charge vs block
facts.fact: A charge is called when the defender is stationary or moving backward with both feet on the floor and takes contact in the torso; if he is still moving into position it is a blocking foul.

facts.subject: scoring values
facts.fact: A field goal from on or inside the three-point line counts two points, one from outside it counts three, and a free throw counts one.

facts.subject: players on court
facts.fact: Five players from each team may be on the court at one time in standard basketball.
